103	MATERIALS & METHODS
104	Participants
105	This study is a sub-study of a larger randomized controlled trial (RCT), in which the efficacy of two
106	hamstring injury prevention exercises in male basketball players is evaluated by diffusion tensor MRI
107	(Dutch trial register ID: NL7248). The main study consists of three arms of 24 participants: a Control
108	group, NHE intervention and the Diver hamstring exercise intervention. Both the Control group and the
109	NHE intervention group were invited to participate in the present study over the period of accessibility
110	of the laboratory. Participants were recruited from basketball teams and via promotion at sports and
111	hospital facilities as well as social media platforms. Inclusion criteria were 16 years of age or older, male,
112	playing basketball and the exclusion criterion was a hamstring injury within the preceding 12 months. All
113	participants gave written consent before the start of data collection. Study protocol and testing
114	procedure were approved by the medical research ethics committee Academic Medical Center
115	Amsterdam (NL63496.018.17) and were in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.
116	Study preparation
117	Multichannel electromyography & electrode placement
118	Muscle activity distribution was assessed through multichannel EMG. Hamstrings of the left leg were
119	studied to align with a magnetic resonance imaging procedure in the main study. The skin of the
120	posterior thigh was shaved and cleaned with alcohol (70%) before placing electrodes. Starting posture
121	for electrode placement were in accordance with the SENIAM guidelines.30 The participants were lying
122	prone with the knee slightly flexed, to contract the hamstrings in order to distinguish muscle belly from
123	tendon.30 The hamstrings were individually palpated to determine proximal and distal margins of each
124	muscle belly. The superficial anatomical position of the hamstring muscles and low volumes of
125	subcutaneous fat tissue in the participating athletes made manual palpation adequate for identifying
126	individual hamstring muscles.31
127	Fifteen electrode pairs (22x28 mm, Blue Sensor N-00-S, Ambu Medicotest A/S, Ølstykke,
128	Denmark) were uniformly distributed along the proximal-distal axis of each muscle belly: five over the
129	biceps femoris long head, four over the semitendinosus and six over the semimembranosus (Figure 1).
130	The number of electrode pairs per muscle was chosen to cover the skin surface area evenly and in a
131	comparable manner between participants of different body height. The most proximal and distal
132	electrodes were placed against the proximal and distal margins, the remainder was divided with an
133	equal distance between electrode pairs per muscle. The inter-electrode distance was 22 mm and the
134	distance between pairs depended on the individual’s muscle length. The reference electrode was placed
135	over the left anterior superior iliac spine. Signals were differentially amplified and stored on a computer
136	through a wired connection (Porti7-16bt, TMS International BV, Oldenzaal, the Netherlands; input
137	impedance > 1012 Ω, analogue-digital conversion at 2,000 samples per second, 22-bit resolution). Cables
138	were taped and secured to the leg with a soft foam wrap to minimize movement artefacts.
139	Maximal voluntary isometric contraction
140	Three maximum voluntary isometric contractions (MVIC) were performed for EMG normalization with
141	approximately 30 seconds rest in between. In prone position, 15° knee flexion with the ankle in neutral

143	position, the examiner fixated the foot manually. The participants gradually increased knee flexion effort
144	from rest to maximum and sustained the maximum for approximately three seconds.32 Participants
145	were verbally encouraged to ensure maximal effort.33
146	Motion tracking
147	One Cluster marker on the dorsal side of the sacrum and two cluster markers at the lateral side of the
148	left thigh and left calf were used to assess hip and knee flexion-extension angles. One single marker was
149	placed on the outer side of the shoe, at the height of the lateral head of the fifth metatarsal five to
150	assess foot ground contact. Three-dimensional coordinates were collected with three Optotrak Certus
151	cameras (Northern Digital, Waterloo ON, Canada), surrounding a treadmill (Bonte Technology B.V.,
152	Zwolle, The Netherlands), with global orientation: X; forwards-backwards, Y; left-right, Z; upwards-
153	downwards. The motion capture system collected samples at 100 Hz. Kinematic and EMG recordings
154	were synchronized by a pulse, sent by the motion capture system and received as extra input channel in
155	the EMG system.
156	Data collection
157	Participants wore a safety harness during the high-speed running trials, and were instructed to run in
158	the centre of the treadmill throughout the whole measurement. Participants performed a five-minute
159	warm-up, consisting of jogging on the treadmill at self-selected speed and optionally self-selected
160	stretch exercises. After warm-up, participants were verbally instructed how to run during three
161	experimental trials while muscle activity and kinematic data were collected. Participants were instructed
162	to catch up with a gentle linear acceleration of the treadmill (approximately 0.88 m.s-2), up to a running
163	speed which they subjectively could maintain for maximally 10 seconds. Participants were instructed to
164	verbally express when they reached this running speed, after which an examiner manually terminated
165	the acceleration of the treadmill. The treadmill was then kept at a constant speed for approximately
166	three seconds, after which the treadmill was decelerated.
167	Data analysis
168	Kinematic data
169	The trial with the highest treadmill speed and in field of view of the motion capture cameras was
170	analysed, using MATLAB R2020b (The MathWorks, Natick, MA, United States). Three consecutive strides
171	cycles were manually identified at the highest speed during the phase at which running speed was
172	constant, based on characteristic changes in kinematic time series of the foot marker.5 A distinct pattern
173	was present in the vertical displacement of the foot marker (e.g. toe-off was identified as a constant
174	value of vertical displacement). A stride cycle was defined from toe-off, to the next toe-off of the same
175	foot.34 Hip joint angles were calculated from the cluster marker on the pelvis and thigh, using Euler
176	decomposition in the order Y-X-Z (sagittal plane flexion–coronal plane flexion–transverse plane
177	rotation).35 Knee joint angles were calculated from the cluster markers on the thigh and calf, using Euler
178	decomposition in the order Y–X–Z (sagittal plane flexion–coronal plane flexion–transverse plane
179	rotation).35 Per stride cycle, three phases were determined: early-swing; from toe-off to maximum knee
180	flexion, late-swing; from maximum knee flexion to heel-strike, stance; from heel-strike to toe-off.

182	Electromyographic data
183	For multichannel EMG data, both MVIC and run recordings were processed with a bi-directional second
184	order Butterworth band-pass filter of 25-500Hz, rectification and a bi-directional second order
185	Butterworth low-pass filter of 25 Hz. The maximum value of a single sample of EMG activity in the three
186	MVIC attempts of each electrode location, was used for normalization of the signal of the corresponding
187	electrode location during the run trial (EMG in percentage maximal voluntary isometric contraction,
188	%MVIC).36 Different cutoff frequencies for the band-pass filter are presented in Supplementary Figure 1.
189	Individual phases of three consecutive strides were extracted from the multichannel EMG. Data
190	were time normalized per stride cycle (100 data samples over a complete stride, 0 – 100%), with the
191	relative duration of the early-swing, late-swing and stance phase set at a fixed percentage per phase,
192	determined as the ratio of the group average duration of the individual phases with respect to the total
193	stride duration. The group averaged absolute durations of the three phases were 0.22 ± 0.02, 0.20 ±
194	0.02 and 0.11 ± 0.01 s for the early-swing, late-swing and stance phase respectively. The stride cycle (1-
195	100%) was accordingly divided in the following relative durations: 1-42% stride cycle for the early-swing
196	phase, 43-80% stride cycle for the late-swing phase and 81-100% stride cycle for the stance phase.
197	Detailed results of individual absolute durations are presented in Supplementary Table 1. Periods with
198	evident contamination (e.g. movement artefacts) in the raw EMG data over the three strides were
199	manually labelled as NaN (not a number) in Matlab to exclude these periods from analysis. Results were
200	averaged over three strides. Per percentage of the stride cycle, muscle average EMG activity were
201	calculated across all electrode locations of the corresponding hamstring muscles (in %MVIC). The
202	relative contribution of individual muscles was assessed as the ratio of the mean normalized of the
203	biceps femoris long head, the semitendinosus and the semimembranosus, to the summated normalized
204	muscle activity of the three muscles (relative contribution (%con) = [individual normalized muscle
205	activity]/[summed normalized muscle activity of all three muscles]).17,37
206	Peak muscle activity
207	Peak EMG activity was calculated over the stride cycle 1) within muscles: at the instant that peak activity
208	occurred for each electrode location per muscle, 2) between muscles: at the instant that the peak
209	activity occurred in the mean activity across the electrode locations per muscle, 3) over the total
210	hamstring muscle: at the instant that the peak activity occurred in the mean over all 15 electrode
211	locations. For each time-point of peak EMG activity, the associated hip and knee joint angles were
212	extracted from the kinematic time series, in degrees.27 Full leg extension was 0°, with positive values for
213	flexion of the hip and knee joint.
214	Statistical analysis
215	One-dimensional statistical parametric mapping (SPM) was used to test for differences in muscle activity
216	between electrode locations within individual muscles and between muscles.38 The whole stride cycle
217	(1-100%) was used as one input. Repeated measures ANOVAs for one-dimensional measures were used
218	to test for differences between electrode locations for each muscle individually, with electrode location
219	as a factor and normalized muscle activity (%MVIC) as dependent variable. Repeated measures ANOVAs

239	Data collection & participant characteristics
240	The inclusion period for this study was 13 months, while the window of inclusion for the main study was
241	19 months. Within this 13-months period, 38 of the total included 48 participants of the larger RCT could
242	participate. One of the 38 participants did not show up at the scheduled time slot. Eight measured data
243	sets were not suitable for analysis, as pelvis and foot markers were recorded improperly. Data sets of 29
244	participants were used for analysis. The mean age was 17 ± 1 yr.; mass, 85 ± 9 kg; height, 193 ± 9 cm;
245	maximal running speed, 7.6 ± 0.5 m.s-1. Two participants suffered an anterior cruciate ligament (ACL)
246	injury of the left leg in the past: one treated non-surgically and one with a semitendinosus tendon graft
247	reconstruction. Four cases of evident contamination were observed in the raw EMG data sets of four
248	individual participants: once the second most distal electrode location of the semitendinosus, once the
249	most proximal electrode location of the semimembranosus and twice the most distal electrode location
250	of the semimembranosus. The episodes containing these contaminations were discarded and are
251	illustrated in Supplementary Figures 2 to 5.
252	Distribution of activity within muscles
253	Within the biceps femoris long head, there was a significant main effect of electrode location on
254	normalized muscle activity (df(4,112), F = 4.68, p < 0.05, Figure 2A-B). This effect occurred in the early-
255	swing, late-swing and stance phases. Post hoc tests revealed that the most proximal electrode location
256	had a higher normalized muscle activity compared to all other electrode locations. Both the second most
257	distal and most distal electrode location had a higher normalized muscle activity compared to the
258	second most proximal and middle electrode in the early-swing phase. A more detailed description of the
259	post hoc tests for the biceps femoris long head is illustrated in Supplementary Figure 6.

261	normalized muscle activity (df(3,84), F = 5.65, p < 0.05, Figure 2C-D). Post hoc tests revealed that the
262	second most proximal electrode location had a lower normalized muscle activity compared to the most
263	proximal and second most distal electrode location in the late-swing phase. A more detailed description
264	of the post hoc tests for the semitendinosus is illustrated in Supplementary Figure 7.

297	DISCUSSION
298	In this study, hamstring muscle activity and relative contribution were assessed with multichannel EMG
299	over a stride cycle during high-speed running in uninjured male basketball players. The main findings
300	were that during the late-swing phase (i) when normalized muscle activity was the highest, the
301	semimembranosus muscle activity was significantly higher than the semitendinosus, (ii) there was
302	heterogeneous activity within the biceps femoris long head, the semitendinosus and the
303	semimembranosus, and (iii) peak EMG activity occurred at comparable hip and knee joint angles for all
304	three hamstring muscles.
305	Compared to literature
306	Hamstring muscle activity during high-speed running was previously assessed with multichannel
307	EMG for the biceps femoris long head and semitendinosus.23,25 These two studies investigated primarily
308	the effect of running speed on the amplitude of normalized muscle activity within each muscle.23,25 One
309	of these studies reported within hamstring muscle activity distribution as a sub-analysis.25 In contrast to
310	our findings, no differences were found among three regions within the biceps femoris long head and
311	semitendinosus, when comparing muscle activity over a stride cycle during high-speed running.25 One of
312	multiple possible explanations is that heterogeneous activity was possibly averaged out in the
313	aforementioned study, as means were calculated over multiple EMG channels to form three regions per
314	muscle. Our results indicate heterogeneous muscle activity within the hamstring muscles if assessed
315	using a configuration with multiple regions during high-speed running. There was also a difference in
316	what MVIC was used for normalization of the signal, which probably resulted in lower normalized EMG
317	activity in our study. The maximum value of a single sample was used in our study probably resulted in a
318	relatively lower normalized EMG activity (Figure 2 & 3) compared to an averaged value over a 1-s epoch
319	in the aforementioned study.25 For comparisons between muscles, existing literature is limited to single
320	channel EMG studies.28,39,40 None of these studies evaluated the semimembranosus activity.28,39,40 In the
321	early-swing phase, studies described a significantly higher muscle activity in the semitendinosus
322	compared to the biceps femoris long, which is in contrast to our results.28,39,40 A possible explanation can
323	be the heterogeneous activity distribution within the individual hamstring muscles. We measured higher
324	normalized muscle activity in the proximal and distal regions of the biceps femoris long head during the
325	early-swing phase compared to the middle electrode location, which roughly corresponds to the
326	electrode location used in the aforementioned studies.28,39,40 In the late-swing phase, no significant
327	differences between the muscle activity of the biceps femoris long head and semitendinosus during
328	high-speed running were reported, which is in line with our results.28,39,40 An interesting observation in
329	our results was the decrease of mean normalized muscle activity of all three hamstring muscles just
330	before heel-strike, at the end of the late-swing phase (Figure 3). Here, the semitendinosus and
331	semimembranosus activity decreased rapidly, while the biceps femoris long head remained more active
332	into the stance phase. This effect was statistically significant when comparing relative contributions
333	between muscles (Figure 4), yet not when looking at normalized muscle activity (Figure 3). The higher
334	contribution of the biceps femoris long head in the late-swing phase was possibly again caused by the
335	heterogeneous activity of this muscle. The most proximal electrode location showed again significantly
336	higher normalized muscle activity in the late-swing phase compared to the two distal electrode location.
337	This proximal location corresponds to the most frequently injured location within the biceps femoris

339	long head.41,42 This is also the phase during high-speed running and location within the biceps femoris
340	long head with the highest strain according to model studies.43,44 It would be interesting to examine
341	neural drive between the hamstring muscles in the late-swing phase during high-speed running and the
342	relationship between activity levels in the proximal region of the biceps femoris long head and injury
343	occurrence.45,46
344	Hip and knee joint angles at peak EMG activity for different electrode location did not differ
345	significantly. All peak EMG activities, both within individual muscles as well as over the mean of each of
346	the muscles, occurred in the late-swing phase. These results corresponds to results of a previous study
347	in which the peak EMG activity was compared between sprinting and a variety of hamstring exercises for
348	individual hamstring muscles.27 The reported hip and joint angles at peak EMG activity of the biceps
349	femoris long head, semitendinosus and semimembranosus were within one standard deviation of our
350	results.27 All peak EMG activities occurred at high musculotendinous length, when the hamstring
351	muscles perform the largest amount of negative work.6 This indicates that high muscle activity, muscle
352	strain and negative power coincide and may explain why the late-swing phase is associated with
353	hamstring injury occurrence.
354	The strength of this study is the use of multichannel EMG, compared to single electrode usage.
355	It has previously been shown that heterogeneous muscle activity can cause an over- or underestimation
356	when using conventional single-channel EMG recordings.24,26 To highlight the importance, we repeated
357	the between hamstring analyses with the electrode location per muscle which corresponded most to
358	the SENIAM guidelines.30 As a result, the between-muscle difference in normalized muscle activity in the
359	late-swing phase disappeared (see Supplementary Figure 13). This observation, especially because it
360	appears in the late-swing phase, signifies the additional value of using multiple EMG channels per
361	muscle. Future studies should confirm this by comparing multichannel EMG with SENIAM guidelines.
362	Limitations
363	One of the limitations of this study is that inclusion was restricted to uninjured basketball players, which
364	might limit generalizability to other and injured athletes. Furthermore, an inherent limitation of using
365	EMG is cross-talk between muscles. With multichannel EMG, electrode locations are closer to proximal
366	and distal muscle borders compared to conventional EMG, which may be more prone to crosstalk. Given
367	the expertise in clinical care and based on comparisons with MRI in the larger RCT, manual palpation
368	was considered accurate for identifying hamstring muscles. By careful electrode placement over the
369	targeted muscle belly, minimizing inter-electrode to 22 mm and using differential amplification, cross-
370	talk and electrode placement over tendon was minimized as much as possible, but cannot be completely
371	ruled out. It is furthermore unknown to what extent the influence is of the tendinous inscription within
372	the semitendinosus and electrode displacement by skin displacement because of movement.47 Future
373	studies should consider obtaining multiple MVIC values for normalization over a variety of hip and knee
374	joint angles, as a single MVIC can result in a fractional under- or overestimation of normalized muscle
375	activity.48 The approximately 4 kg extra weight of the safety harness and EMG registration device,
376	attached on the backside of the harness, had an unknown effect on the posture of the participants
377	during high-speed running. We did not exclude the participants with a history of a hamstring injury,
378	older than 12 months, or participants who had a history of ACL reconstruction with semitendinosus
379	tendon graft. They might have long-lasting effects on hamstring muscle activity and should be

381	considered when assessing unilateral muscle activity.49-52 Finally, participants were tested on a treadmill
382	and not in overground running to allow data acquisition. Treadmill-based running analysis is comparable
383	to over ground running and had as benefit that running speed can be regulated effectively.53
384	Conclusion
385	This study comprehensively described the distribution of hamstring muscle activity during high-speed
386	running, both within and between muscles. Our findings were that (i) when the hamstring muscles were
387	most active during high-speed running, in the late-swing phase, the semimembranosus was most active,
388	(ii) contrasting, the semitendinosus was least active in the late-swing phase during high-speed running,
389	(iii) within the biceps femoris long head, the most proximal region was significantly more active in the
390	late-swing phase, compared to other muscle regions, and (iv) peak muscle activity, assessed locally
391	within individual hamstring muscles, as well as in general over the whole muscle, occurred at similar hip
392	and knee joint angles during high-speed running.
393	Perspective
394	The present study provides novel information about the distribution of muscle activity of the hamstring
395	muscles during high-speed running. This comprehensive study showed that when the hamstring muscles
396	are most active, in the late-swing phase, the level of muscle activity of the semimembranosus is
397	significantly higher compared to the semitendinosus. Also in the late-swing phase during high-speed
398	running, the level of muscle activity in the most proximal part of the biceps femoris long head was
399	significantly more active compared to other regions within the same muscle. This location within the
400	biceps femoris long head corresponds to the most injurious area of the hamstring muscle. Peaks in
401	muscle activity occurred at similar hip and knee joint angles during high-speed running. Future studies
402	should examine if preventive interventions have an effect on the activity distribution during high-speed
403	running.

ABSTRACT
Purpose
This study assessed activity distribution among the hamstring muscles during high-speed running. The
objective was to compare within and between muscle activity, relative contribution and hip and knee
joint angles at peak muscle activity during high-speed running.
Methods
Through multichannel electromyography, we measured muscle activity in male basketball players during
high-speed running on a treadmill at 15 locations: five for biceps femoris long head, four for
semitendinosus, six for semimembranosus. Muscle activity was calculated for each location within each
hamstring muscle individually for each percent of a stride cycle.
Results
Twenty-nine non-injured basketball players were included (mean age: 17 ± 1 years; mass, 85 ± 9 kg;
height, 193 ± 9 cm). Heterogeneous activity was found for all individual hamstring muscles across
multiple events of the stride cycle. In the late-swing phase, muscle activity and relative contribution of
the semimembranosus was significantly higher than of the semitendinosus. There was no significant
difference in hip and knee joint angles at instant of peak muscle activity, assessed locally within
individual hamstring muscles, as well as in general over the whole hamstring muscle.
Conclusion
Hamstring muscles were most active in the late-swing phase during high-speed running. In this phase,
the semimembranosus was most active and the semitendinosus was least active. Within the biceps
femoris long head, the most proximal region was significantly more active in the late-swing phase,
compared to other muscle regions. For each muscle and location, peak muscle activity occurred at
similar hip and knee joint angles.

INTRODUCTION
Hamstring injuries are the most prevalent type of injuries in sports, generally occurring during high-
speed running.1-4 It has been suggested that the bi-articular hamstring muscles (biceps femoris long
head, semitendinosus and semimembranosus) are most susceptible to injury during the late-swing
phase of the stride cycle of high-speed running.5-7 According to computational models, forces produced
by the hamstring muscles are peaking in the late swing, simultaneously with high velocity muscle
lengthening.8-11 These muscles are accountable for the deceleration of hip flexion and knee extension,8-11
and thus absorb high levels of eccentric mechanical load during the late swing phase.
A high contribution of biceps femoris long head during strenuous exercise compared to the
semitendinosus and semimembranosus was associated with an increased risk of a first-time injury.12 It
has been suggested that hamstring injuries occur because of an inadequate distribution of individual
contributions of hamstring muscles, also known as load sharing.12,13 Load sharing refers to the
distribution of muscle forces in a synergistic muscle group to jointly produce a joint moment.14 Forces
exerted by individual muscle and thus load sharing cannot be assessed non-invasively in vivo.
Distribution of muscle activity has therefore previously been used as a proxy of load sharing.15 Previous
studies successfully assessed muscle activity through surface electromyography (EMG),16 functional
magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) 12,17,18 and shear wave elastography.19,20 A relatively high activity of
the semitendinosus may protect against injury, possibly because it would unload the most frequently
affected long head of the biceps femoris.17,21,22 Additional information regarding load sharing between
hamstring muscles during high-speed running may provide new information on the aetiology of
hamstring injuries.
It has previously been reported that activation patterns differ both within and between the
biceps femoris long head and semitendinosus during high-speed running and various exercises.23-26 On
average, peak muscle activity during high-speed running occurs in the late swing phase, yet muscle
activation patterns between hamstring muscles differ substantially between athletes.25,27 Running speed
seems to have an influence on both the amplitude and timing of muscle activity: amplitude increases
with increasing running speed,25,28 and at near maximum running speed, peak activity of the biceps
femoris long head compared to the semitendinosus is delayed.28 While the amplitude of muscle activity
within individual hamstring muscles can be heterogeneous,23-26 it is unknown whether regional peaks of
this amplitude within individual muscles occur at the same hip and knee joint angles. A better
understanding of peak muscle activation patterns within and between hamstring muscles is required to
provide more insight into the aetiology of hamstring injuries. Furthermore, (distribution of) EMG activity
within the semimembranosus over the different phases of a stride cycle during high-speed running has
not previously been reported. Especially for larger muscles as the hamstrings, the application of
multichannel EMG would be an appropriate method.29
The aims of this descriptive study were; 1) to asses muscle activity within and between the three
hamstring muscles (biceps femoris long head, semitendinosus and semimembranosus) over one stride
cycle during high-speed running, 2) to investigate the relative contribution between muscles, and 3) to
evaluate hip and knee joint angles at instants of peak muscle activity within and between the three
individual hamstring muscles.

MATERIALS & METHODS
Participants
This study is a sub-study of a larger randomized controlled trial (RCT), in which the efficacy of two
hamstring injury prevention exercises in male basketball players is evaluated by diffusion tensor MRI
(Dutch trial register ID: NL7248). The main study consists of three arms of 24 participants: a Control
group, NHE intervention and the Diver hamstring exercise intervention. Both the Control group and the
NHE intervention group were invited to participate in the present study over the period of accessibility
of the laboratory. Participants were recruited from basketball teams and via promotion at sports and
hospital facilities as well as social media platforms. Inclusion criteria were 16 years of age or older, male,
playing basketball and the exclusion criterion was a hamstring injury within the preceding 12 months. All
participants gave written consent before the start of data collection. Study protocol and testing
procedure were approved by the medical research ethics committee Academic Medical Center
Amsterdam (NL63496.018.17) and were in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.
Study preparation
Multichannel electromyography & electrode placement
Muscle activity distribution was assessed through multichannel EMG. Hamstrings of the left leg were
studied to align with a magnetic resonance imaging procedure in the main study. The skin of the
posterior thigh was shaved and cleaned with alcohol (70%) before placing electrodes. Starting posture
for electrode placement were in accordance with the SENIAM guidelines.30 The participants were lying
prone with the knee slightly flexed, to contract the hamstrings in order to distinguish muscle belly from
tendon.30 The hamstrings were individually palpated to determine proximal and distal margins of each
muscle belly. The superficial anatomical position of the hamstring muscles and low volumes of
subcutaneous fat tissue in the participating athletes made manual palpation adequate for identifying
individual hamstring muscles.31
Fifteen electrode pairs (22x28 mm, Blue Sensor N-00-S, Ambu Medicotest A/S, Ølstykke,
Denmark) were uniformly distributed along the proximal-distal axis of each muscle belly: five over the
biceps femoris long head, four over the semitendinosus and six over the semimembranosus (Figure 1).
The number of electrode pairs per muscle was chosen to cover the skin surface area evenly and in a
comparable manner between participants of different body height. The most proximal and distal
electrodes were placed against the proximal and distal margins, the remainder was divided with an
equal distance between electrode pairs per muscle. The inter-electrode distance was 22 mm and the
distance between pairs depended on the individual’s muscle length. The reference electrode was placed
over the left anterior superior iliac spine. Signals were differentially amplified and stored on a computer
through a wired connection (Porti7-16bt, TMS International BV, Oldenzaal, the Netherlands; input
impedance > 1012 Ω, analogue-digital conversion at 2,000 samples per second, 22-bit resolution). Cables
were taped and secured to the leg with a soft foam wrap to minimize movement artefacts.
Maximal voluntary isometric contraction
Three maximum voluntary isometric contractions (MVIC) were performed for EMG normalization with
approximately 30 seconds rest in between. In prone position, 15° knee flexion with the ankle in neutral

Motion tracking
One Cluster marker on the dorsal side of the sacrum and two cluster markers at the lateral side of the
left thigh and left calf were used to assess hip and knee flexion-extension angles. One single marker was
placed on the outer side of the shoe, at the height of the lateral head of the fifth metatarsal five to
assess foot ground contact. Three-dimensional coordinates were collected with three Optotrak Certus
cameras (Northern Digital, Waterloo ON, Canada), surrounding a treadmill (Bonte Technology B.V.,
Zwolle, The Netherlands), with global orientation: X; forwards-backwards, Y; left-right, Z; upwards-
downwards. The motion capture system collected samples at 100 Hz. Kinematic and EMG recordings
were synchronized by a pulse, sent by the motion capture system and received as extra input channel in
the EMG system.
Data collection
Participants wore a safety harness during the high-speed running trials, and were instructed to run in
the centre of the treadmill throughout the whole measurement. Participants performed a five-minute
warm-up, consisting of jogging on the treadmill at self-selected speed and optionally self-selected
stretch exercises. After warm-up, participants were verbally instructed how to run during three
experimental trials while muscle activity and kinematic data were collected. Participants were instructed
to catch up with a gentle linear acceleration of the treadmill (approximately 0.88 m.s-2), up to a running
speed which they subjectively could maintain for maximally 10 seconds. Participants were instructed to
verbally express when they reached this running speed, after which an examiner manually terminated
the acceleration of the treadmill. The treadmill was then kept at a constant speed for approximately
three seconds, after which the treadmill was decelerated.
Data analysis
Kinematic data
The trial with the highest treadmill speed and in field of view of the motion capture cameras was
analysed, using MATLAB R2020b (The MathWorks, Natick, MA, United States). Three consecutive strides
cycles were manually identified at the highest speed during the phase at which running speed was
constant, based on characteristic changes in kinematic time series of the foot marker.5 A distinct pattern
was present in the vertical displacement of the foot marker (e.g. toe-off was identified as a constant
value of vertical displacement). A stride cycle was defined from toe-off, to the next toe-off of the same
foot.34 Hip joint angles were calculated from the cluster marker on the pelvis and thigh, using Euler
decomposition in the order Y-X-Z (sagittal plane flexion–coronal plane flexion–transverse plane
rotation).35 Knee joint angles were calculated from the cluster markers on the thigh and calf, using Euler
decomposition in the order Y–X–Z (sagittal plane flexion–coronal plane flexion–transverse plane
rotation).35 Per stride cycle, three phases were determined: early-swing; from toe-off to maximum knee
flexion, late-swing; from maximum knee flexion to heel-strike, stance; from heel-strike to toe-off.

Electromyographic data
For multichannel EMG data, both MVIC and run recordings were processed with a bi-directional second
order Butterworth band-pass filter of 25-500Hz, rectification and a bi-directional second order
Butterworth low-pass filter of 25 Hz. The maximum value of a single sample of EMG activity in the three
MVIC attempts of each electrode location, was used for normalization of the signal of the corresponding
electrode location during the run trial (EMG in percentage maximal voluntary isometric contraction,
%MVIC).36 Different cutoff frequencies for the band-pass filter are presented in Supplementary Figure 1.
Individual phases of three consecutive strides were extracted from the multichannel EMG. Data
were time normalized per stride cycle (100 data samples over a complete stride, 0 – 100%), with the
relative duration of the early-swing, late-swing and stance phase set at a fixed percentage per phase,
determined as the ratio of the group average duration of the individual phases with respect to the total
stride duration. The group averaged absolute durations of the three phases were 0.22 ± 0.02, 0.20 ±
0.02 and 0.11 ± 0.01 s for the early-swing, late-swing and stance phase respectively. The stride cycle (1-
100%) was accordingly divided in the following relative durations: 1-42% stride cycle for the early-swing
phase, 43-80% stride cycle for the late-swing phase and 81-100% stride cycle for the stance phase.
Detailed results of individual absolute durations are presented in Supplementary Table 1. Periods with
evident contamination (e.g. movement artefacts) in the raw EMG data over the three strides were
manually labelled as NaN (not a number) in Matlab to exclude these periods from analysis. Results were
averaged over three strides. Per percentage of the stride cycle, muscle average EMG activity were
calculated across all electrode locations of the corresponding hamstring muscles (in %MVIC). The
relative contribution of individual muscles was assessed as the ratio of the mean normalized of the
biceps femoris long head, the semitendinosus and the semimembranosus, to the summated normalized
muscle activity of the three muscles (relative contribution (%con) = [individual normalized muscle
activity]/[summed normalized muscle activity of all three muscles]).17,37
Peak muscle activity
Peak EMG activity was calculated over the stride cycle 1) within muscles: at the instant that peak activity
occurred for each electrode location per muscle, 2) between muscles: at the instant that the peak
activity occurred in the mean activity across the electrode locations per muscle, 3) over the total
hamstring muscle: at the instant that the peak activity occurred in the mean over all 15 electrode
locations. For each time-point of peak EMG activity, the associated hip and knee joint angles were
extracted from the kinematic time series, in degrees.27 Full leg extension was 0°, with positive values for
flexion of the hip and knee joint.
Statistical analysis
One-dimensional statistical parametric mapping (SPM) was used to test for differences in muscle activity
between electrode locations within individual muscles and between muscles.38 The whole stride cycle
(1-100%) was used as one input. Repeated measures ANOVAs for one-dimensional measures were used
to test for differences between electrode locations for each muscle individually, with electrode location
as a factor and normalized muscle activity (%MVIC) as dependent variable. Repeated measures ANOVAs

RESULTS
Data collection & participant characteristics
The inclusion period for this study was 13 months, while the window of inclusion for the main study was
19 months. Within this 13-months period, 38 of the total included 48 participants of the larger RCT could
participate. One of the 38 participants did not show up at the scheduled time slot. Eight measured data
sets were not suitable for analysis, as pelvis and foot markers were recorded improperly. Data sets of 29
participants were used for analysis. The mean age was 17 ± 1 yr.; mass, 85 ± 9 kg; height, 193 ± 9 cm;
maximal running speed, 7.6 ± 0.5 m.s-1. Two participants suffered an anterior cruciate ligament (ACL)
injury of the left leg in the past: one treated non-surgically and one with a semitendinosus tendon graft
reconstruction. Four cases of evident contamination were observed in the raw EMG data sets of four
individual participants: once the second most distal electrode location of the semitendinosus, once the
most proximal electrode location of the semimembranosus and twice the most distal electrode location
of the semimembranosus. The episodes containing these contaminations were discarded and are
illustrated in Supplementary Figures 2 to 5.
Distribution of activity within muscles
Within the biceps femoris long head, there was a significant main effect of electrode location on
normalized muscle activity (df(4,112), F = 4.68, p < 0.05, Figure 2A-B). This effect occurred in the early-
swing, late-swing and stance phases. Post hoc tests revealed that the most proximal electrode location
had a higher normalized muscle activity compared to all other electrode locations. Both the second most
distal and most distal electrode location had a higher normalized muscle activity compared to the
second most proximal and middle electrode in the early-swing phase. A more detailed description of the
post hoc tests for the biceps femoris long head is illustrated in Supplementary Figure 6.
Within the semitendinosus, there was a significant main effect of electrode location on
normalized muscle activity (df(3,84), F = 5.65, p < 0.05, Figure 2C-D). Post hoc tests revealed that the
second most proximal electrode location had a lower normalized muscle activity compared to the most
proximal and second most distal electrode location in the late-swing phase. A more detailed description
of the post hoc tests for the semitendinosus is illustrated in Supplementary Figure 7.
Within the semimembranosus, there was a significant main effect of electrode location on
normalized muscle activity (df(5,140), F = 4.19, p < 0.05, Figure 2E-F). This effect occurred in the early-
swing and late-swing phase. Post hoc tests revealed that the most distal electrode locations had a higher
normalized muscle activity compared to all other electrode locations in the early swing-phase. The
second most distal electrode location had a higher normalized muscle activity compared to the third
most proximal, second most proximal and third most distal electrode location in the early-swing phase.
A more detailed description of the post hoc tests for the semimembranosus is illustrated in
Supplementary Figure 8. Individual hamstring muscle distributions per participant are illustrated in
Supplementary Figure 11.

Between muscles, the overall normalized muscle activity over one stride cycle during high-speed running
differed significantly in the early-swing phase, late-swing phase and over the transition between stance
to early-swing phase (df(2,56), F = 7.31, p < 0.05, Figure 3A-B). Post hoc tests revealed that the

DISCUSSION
In this study, hamstring muscle activity and relative contribution were assessed with multichannel EMG
over a stride cycle during high-speed running in uninjured male basketball players. The main findings
were that during the late-swing phase (i) when normalized muscle activity was the highest, the
semimembranosus muscle activity was significantly higher than the semitendinosus, (ii) there was
heterogeneous activity within the biceps femoris long head, the semitendinosus and the
semimembranosus, and (iii) peak EMG activity occurred at comparable hip and knee joint angles for all
three hamstring muscles.
Compared to literature
Hamstring muscle activity during high-speed running was previously assessed with multichannel
EMG for the biceps femoris long head and semitendinosus.23,25 These two studies investigated primarily
the effect of running speed on the amplitude of normalized muscle activity within each muscle.23,25 One
of these studies reported within hamstring muscle activity distribution as a sub-analysis.25 In contrast to
our findings, no differences were found among three regions within the biceps femoris long head and
semitendinosus, when comparing muscle activity over a stride cycle during high-speed running.25 One of
multiple possible explanations is that heterogeneous activity was possibly averaged out in the
aforementioned study, as means were calculated over multiple EMG channels to form three regions per
muscle. Our results indicate heterogeneous muscle activity within the hamstring muscles if assessed
using a configuration with multiple regions during high-speed running. There was also a difference in
what MVIC was used for normalization of the signal, which probably resulted in lower normalized EMG
activity in our study. The maximum value of a single sample was used in our study probably resulted in a
relatively lower normalized EMG activity (Figure 2 & 3) compared to an averaged value over a 1-s epoch
in the aforementioned study.25 For comparisons between muscles, existing literature is limited to single
channel EMG studies.28,39,40 None of these studies evaluated the semimembranosus activity.28,39,40 In the
early-swing phase, studies described a significantly higher muscle activity in the semitendinosus
compared to the biceps femoris long, which is in contrast to our results.28,39,40 A possible explanation can
be the heterogeneous activity distribution within the individual hamstring muscles. We measured higher
normalized muscle activity in the proximal and distal regions of the biceps femoris long head during the
early-swing phase compared to the middle electrode location, which roughly corresponds to the
electrode location used in the aforementioned studies.28,39,40 In the late-swing phase, no significant
differences between the muscle activity of the biceps femoris long head and semitendinosus during
high-speed running were reported, which is in line with our results.28,39,40 An interesting observation in
our results was the decrease of mean normalized muscle activity of all three hamstring muscles just
before heel-strike, at the end of the late-swing phase (Figure 3). Here, the semitendinosus and
semimembranosus activity decreased rapidly, while the biceps femoris long head remained more active
into the stance phase. This effect was statistically significant when comparing relative contributions
between muscles (Figure 4), yet not when looking at normalized muscle activity (Figure 3). The higher
contribution of the biceps femoris long head in the late-swing phase was possibly again caused by the
heterogeneous activity of this muscle. The most proximal electrode location showed again significantly
higher normalized muscle activity in the late-swing phase compared to the two distal electrode location.
This proximal location corresponds to the most frequently injured location within the biceps femoris

long head with the highest strain according to model studies.43,44 It would be interesting to examine

Hip and knee joint angles at peak EMG activity for different electrode location did not differ
significantly. All peak EMG activities, both within individual muscles as well as over the mean of each of
the muscles, occurred in the late-swing phase. These results corresponds to results of a previous study
in which the peak EMG activity was compared between sprinting and a variety of hamstring exercises for
individual hamstring muscles.27 The reported hip and joint angles at peak EMG activity of the biceps
femoris long head, semitendinosus and semimembranosus were within one standard deviation of our
results.27 All peak EMG activities occurred at high musculotendinous length, when the hamstring
muscles perform the largest amount of negative work.6 This indicates that high muscle activity, muscle
strain and negative power coincide and may explain why the late-swing phase is associated with
hamstring injury occurrence.
The strength of this study is the use of multichannel EMG, compared to single electrode usage.
It has previously been shown that heterogeneous muscle activity can cause an over- or underestimation
when using conventional single-channel EMG recordings.24,26 To highlight the importance, we repeated
the between hamstring analyses with the electrode location per muscle which corresponded most to
the SENIAM guidelines.30 As a result, the between-muscle difference in normalized muscle activity in the
late-swing phase disappeared (see Supplementary Figure 13). This observation, especially because it
appears in the late-swing phase, signifies the additional value of using multiple EMG channels per
muscle. Future studies should confirm this by comparing multichannel EMG with SENIAM guidelines.
Limitations
One of the limitations of this study is that inclusion was restricted to uninjured basketball players, which
might limit generalizability to other and injured athletes. Furthermore, an inherent limitation of using
EMG is cross-talk between muscles. With multichannel EMG, electrode locations are closer to proximal
and distal muscle borders compared to conventional EMG, which may be more prone to crosstalk. Given
the expertise in clinical care and based on comparisons with MRI in the larger RCT, manual palpation
was considered accurate for identifying hamstring muscles. By careful electrode placement over the
targeted muscle belly, minimizing inter-electrode to 22 mm and using differential amplification, cross-
talk and electrode placement over tendon was minimized as much as possible, but cannot be completely
ruled out. It is furthermore unknown to what extent the influence is of the tendinous inscription within
the semitendinosus and electrode displacement by skin displacement because of movement.47 Future
studies should consider obtaining multiple MVIC values for normalization over a variety of hip and knee
joint angles, as a single MVIC can result in a fractional under- or overestimation of normalized muscle
activity.48 The approximately 4 kg extra weight of the safety harness and EMG registration device,
attached on the backside of the harness, had an unknown effect on the posture of the participants
during high-speed running. We did not exclude the participants with a history of a hamstring injury,
older than 12 months, or participants who had a history of ACL reconstruction with semitendinosus
tendon graft. They might have long-lasting effects on hamstring muscle activity and should be

Conclusion
This study comprehensively described the distribution of hamstring muscle activity during high-speed
running, both within and between muscles. Our findings were that (i) when the hamstring muscles were
most active during high-speed running, in the late-swing phase, the semimembranosus was most active,
(ii) contrasting, the semitendinosus was least active in the late-swing phase during high-speed running,
(iii) within the biceps femoris long head, the most proximal region was significantly more active in the
late-swing phase, compared to other muscle regions, and (iv) peak muscle activity, assessed locally
within individual hamstring muscles, as well as in general over the whole muscle, occurred at similar hip
and knee joint angles during high-speed running.
Perspective
The present study provides novel information about the distribution of muscle activity of the hamstring
muscles during high-speed running. This comprehensive study showed that when the hamstring muscles
are most active, in the late-swing phase, the level of muscle activity of the semimembranosus is
significantly higher compared to the semitendinosus. Also in the late-swing phase during high-speed
running, the level of muscle activity in the most proximal part of the biceps femoris long head was
significantly more active compared to other regions within the same muscle. This location within the
biceps femoris long head corresponds to the most injurious area of the hamstring muscle. Peaks in
muscle activity occurred at similar hip and knee joint angles during high-speed running. Future studies
should examine if preventive interventions have an effect on the activity distribution during high-speed
running.

 "sourceFile":"A biopsychosocial model for understanding training load, fatigue, and musculoskeletal sport injury in university athletes - A scoping review.pdf",
 "decision":"INCLUDE",

 "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"Title in text 'A Biopsychosocial Model for Understanding Training Load, Fatigue, and Musculoskeletal Sport Injury in University Athletes: A Scoping Review' matches the filename and the Crossref title; authors McClean ZJ et al., J Strength Cond Res.",
 "confidence":"high",
 "studyDesign":"Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
 "primaryDomain":"Sports Medicine & Injury",
 "domains":["Sports Medicine & Injury","Training & Performance","Recovery & Readiness"],
 "audiences":["Sports Medicine","Athletic Training","Performance","Research & Analytics"],
 "sports":["American Football","Soccer","Basketball","Baseball / Softball","Other Sport"],
 "populations":["Collegiate","Male Athletes","Female Athletes"],
 "evidenceSummary":"A scoping review (PRISMA-ScR) of 10 peer-reviewed studies of university athletes, 9 NCAA and 1 U Sports, with 319 participants of whom 14.1% were female. Seven studies examined training load and three examined fatigue, and the authors report that studies linking training load, fatigue and musculoskeletal injury together were scarce and that injury surveillance was inconsistent. They then propose a biopsychosocial injury model from expert consensus, which the review does not test.",
 "screeningLimitations":"Ten small observational studies, mostly NCAA football, were mapped without pooled effect estimates. The proposed model is an expert-consensus construct with no validation data, so it cannot show that the listed factors cause injury.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff may treat the biopsychosocial model (sleep, academic, mental health and social load) as an evidence-based injury risk model, when the review only proposes it as a hypothesis for future research.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2024,
   "citation":"McClean ZJ, Pasanen K, Lun V, Charest J, Herzog W, Werthner P, et al. A Biopsychosocial Model for Understanding Training Load, Fatigue, and Musculoskeletal Sport Injury in University Athletes: A Scoping Review. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2024;38(6):1177-1188.",
   "doi":"10.1519/jsc.0000000000004789",
   "abstract":"The review examined training load, fatigue and musculoskeletal (MSK) injury in university athletes, then used expert consensus to build a biopsychosocial model. Ten articles were included. Key findings were an absence of injury surveillance methodology and contextual factors that can influence the training load-fatigue-MSK injury relationship. The authors highlight academic load, social load and mental health load as key variables and present an integrative model for MSK injury in university sport, with an example of causal inference applied to longitudinal observational data.",
   "tldr":"Few studies of university athletes link training load, fatigue and musculoskeletal injury, and most lack consistent injury surveillance. The biopsychosocial model proposed here is a research framework that still needs to be tested.",
   "methods":"A scoping review following PRISMA-ScR searched Embase, MEDLINE, PubMed and SPORTDiscus in December 2022 for English peer-reviewed studies from 2002 onward on university athletes, MSK injury, training load and fatigue. Two reviewers screened titles, abstracts and full texts independently, and reference lists were checked, giving 10 included articles. Each study was appraised with the Quality Assessment Tool for Observational Cohort and Cross-Sectional Studies, and experts in sport medicine, sleep, sport psychology, biomechanics and sport science reached consensus on eight contextual factors.",
   "findings":"Ten studies were included (9 NCAA, 1 U Sports; 319 participants, 14.1% female). Seven studies examined training load and three examined fatigue. In a tackle football study, injury risk was higher when the acute to chronic workload ratio was 2 SD above or below the individual mean, and greatest at 2 SD above (Sampson et al.). In a basketball cohort of 19 athletes, sleep duration and muscle soreness were significant predictors of injury (Watson et al.). The authors found no study that examined mental health as a predictor of sport injury in university sport.",
   "limitations":"The authors note inconsistent injury surveillance, no control for athlete exposure, no sex- or gender-based analysis, and limited consideration of performance level. Training load was often used as a proxy for tissue load. Most included studies were NCAA football, two studies were female-only, and the fatigue theme mostly measured throwing kinematics rather than injury. The model was not validated against data.",
   "practicalImplications":"For university sport staff, the review supports recording internal and external training load together with wellness, sleep and soreness measures, and using one consistent injury surveillance method, since most studies did not. It also supports including baseline sleep and mental health screening, but no included study tested academic or social load as an injury predictor.",
   "athleteDev":"Limited. The review maps training load and fatigue measures such as session RPE, GPS and inertial load, and wellness questionnaires, but it does not show that any load strategy improves performance. Its performance content is limited to fatigue effects on throwing kinematics and workload in extra time.",
   "rtp":"Limited. The review discusses reinjury and injury etiology, but it does not evaluate return-to-sport criteria or timing. It cannot be used to decide when an athlete is fit to return from injury."
 }
}

15	McClean, ZJ, Pasanen, K, Lun, V, Charest, J, Herzog, W, Werthner, P, Black, A, Vleuten, RV, Lacoste, E, and Jordan, MJ. A
16	biopsychosocial model for understanding training load, fatigue, and musculoskeletal sport injury in university athletes: A scoping
17	review. J Strength Cond Res 38(6): 1177–1188, 2024—The impact of musculoskeletal (MSK) injury on athlete health and per-
18	formance has been studied extensively in youth sport and elite sport. Current research examining the relationship between training
19	load, injury, and fatigue in university athletes is sparse. Furthermore, a range of contextual factors that influence the training load-
20	fatigue-injury relationship exist, necessitating an integrative biopsychosocial model to address primary and secondary injury
21	prevention research. The objectives of this review were (a) to review the scientific literature examining the relationship between
22	training load, fatigue, and MSK injury in university athletes and (b) to use this review in conjunction with a transdisciplinary research
23	team to identify biopsychosocial factors that influence MSK injury and develop an updated, holistic biopsychosocial model to inform
24	injury prevention research and practice in university sport. Ten articles were identified for inclusion in this review. Key findings were
25	an absence of injury surveillance methodology and contextual factors that can influence the training load-fatigue-MSK injury
26	relationship. We highlight the inclusion of academic load, social load, and mental health load as key variables contributing to
27	a multifactorial, gendered environmental, scientific inquiry on sport injury and reinjury in university sport. An integrative biopsy-
28	1WFXFV5EXuVTNVz1wqr/BbBc= on 05/30/2024
29	chosocial model for MSK injury in university sport is presented that can be used to study the biological, psychological, and social
30	factors that modulate injury and reinjury risk in university athletes. Finally, we provide an example of how causal inference can be
31	used to maximize the utility of longitudinally collected observational data that is characteristic of sport performance research in
32	university sport.

McClean, ZJ, Pasanen, K, Lun, V, Charest, J, Herzog, W, Werthner, P, Black, A, Vleuten, RV, Lacoste, E, and Jordan, MJ. A
biopsychosocial model for understanding training load, fatigue, and musculoskeletal sport injury in university athletes: A scoping
review. J Strength Cond Res 38(6): 1177–1188, 2024—The impact of musculoskeletal (MSK) injury on athlete health and per-
formance has been studied extensively in youth sport and elite sport. Current research examining the relationship between training
load, injury, and fatigue in university athletes is sparse. Furthermore, a range of contextual factors that influence the training load-
fatigue-injury relationship exist, necessitating an integrative biopsychosocial model to address primary and secondary injury
prevention research. The objectives of this review were (a) to review the scientific literature examining the relationship between
training load, fatigue, and MSK injury in university athletes and (b) to use this review in conjunction with a transdisciplinary research
team to identify biopsychosocial factors that influence MSK injury and develop an updated, holistic biopsychosocial model to inform
injury prevention research and practice in university sport. Ten articles were identified for inclusion in this review. Key findings were
an absence of injury surveillance methodology and contextual factors that can influence the training load-fatigue-MSK injury
relationship. We highlight the inclusion of academic load, social load, and mental health load as key variables contributing to
a multifactorial, gendered environmental, scientific inquiry on sport injury and reinjury in university sport. An integrative biopsy-

chosocial model for MSK injury in university sport is presented that can be used to study the biological, psychological, and social
factors that modulate injury and reinjury risk in university athletes. Finally, we provide an example of how causal inference can be
used to maximize the utility of longitudinally collected observational data that is characteristic of sport performance research in
university sport.

Note: the externalDoi 10.31236/osf.io/nhqbx appears to be an OSF preprint DOI, while the PDF is the JOSPT article; the operator may wish to replace it.",
 "confidence":"high",
 "studyDesign":"Cohort Study",
 "primaryDomain":"Monitoring & Technology",
 "domains":["Monitoring & Technology","Sports Medicine & Injury","Training & Performance"],
 "audiences":["Research & Analytics","Performance","Sports Medicine"],
 "sports":["Soccer"],
 "populations":["Professional / Elite","Youth / Adolescent","Male Athletes","Female Athletes"],
 "evidenceSummary":"A prospective cohort of 86 elite U-19 football players (47 male, 39 female, from six teams) logged daily training load (session RPE times duration) and health problems for 105 days, recording 196 health problems. Of 108 random-effects analyses of acute:chronic workload ratio (ACWR) variants against three health outcomes, 24 (22%) were significant, most often with EWMA-based ACWR and with low-versus-high comparisons. The authors frame the study as a critique showing that results depend on method choices.",
 "screeningLimitations":"Daily self-report questionnaires that were not validated, with 31% of daily questionnaires unanswered and no adjustment for sex, age or clustering. Since only 22% of the 108 analyses were significant and the authors state the study is not evidence for an ACWR-injury relationship, the paper cannot show that ACWR predicts health problems.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff may read the 24 significant ACWR associations as evidence that ACWR predicts injury, when the authors present the study as a critique of methods and say it is not evidence for that relationship.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2020,
   "citation":"Dalen-Lorentsen T, Andersen TE, Bjørneboe J, Vagle M, Martin KN, Kleppen M, et al. A cherry tree ripe for picking: The relationship between the acute:chronic workload ratio and health problems. Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy. 2020.",
   "doi":"10.31236/osf.io/nhqbx",
   "abstract":"Objective: To investigate whether the relationship between the acute:chronic workload ratio (ACWR) and health problems varies when different methodological approaches are used. Design: Prospective cohort study. Methods: An online questionnaire collected daily health and training data from 86 elite youth footballers for 105 days. ACWR was calculated with 21- and 28-day chronic periods, coupled and uncoupled, exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA) and rolling average, and categorized by pre-defined bins and z-scores; three outcomes were tested in 108 random-effects logistic regression analyses. Results: 6250 training days and 196 health problems were recorded; 24 (22%) of 108 analyses were significant. Conclusions: The relationship between ACWR and health problems depends on methodological choices.",
   "tldr":"In 86 elite youth footballers, 22% of 108 ACWR analysis variants showed a significant link to health problems, and the result depended on how ACWR was calculated and analysed. Treat any single reported ACWR association with caution.",
   "methods":"A prospective cohort of six elite U-19 Norwegian football teams (three girls' and three boys') ran from July to October 2017, covering summer break and 13 to 14 weeks of in-season competition. Players reported daily session duration and RPE by online questionnaire (training load in arbitrary units = duration times RPE) and new or worsening health problems, which a clinician then classified using UEFA guidelines by telephone interview. Twelve ACWR variants were tested against three outcomes (all health problems, all injuries, new non-contact injuries), giving 108 random-effects logistic regression analyses that were not adjusted for sex, age or clustering.",
   "findings":"Of 108 analyses, 24 (22%) were significant. Significant results were most often EWMA-based (15 of 24) and in low-versus-high comparisons (12 of 36, 33%). The largest odds ratio reported in the figure was 5.28 (95% CI 1.83-15.25) for a non-coupled 7:28-day rolling-average z-score ACWR comparing low with high categories, for all injuries.",
   "limitations":"Health problems were self-reported and not medically confirmed, 31% of daily questionnaires were unanswered, and the post-study survey found under-reporting. Several Discussion figures conflict with Table 2, including all health problems (31% in the table vs 33% in the abstract), new non-contact injuries (6% vs 2%), 28-day vs 21-day periods (15% vs 26% significant, the reverse of the text), and coupled vs non-coupled (21% vs 19%); table values are reported here. The text describes the strongest association as coupled 7:21 EWMA (OR 5.27), which does not match the figure, and the PDF prints no publication year, so 2020 comes from the Crossref record.",
   "practicalImplications":"Staff reading ACWR studies should ask whether all analyses were reported and how ACWR was calculated before trusting a single significant result. When collecting data for youth squads, the paper supports recording all health complaints, not only time-loss injuries, but it does not support using ACWR thresholds to manage load.",
   "athleteDev":"Limited. The study does not test whether ACWR-guided load changes improve performance. Its relevance is that calculation choices (period length, rolling average vs EWMA, categories) change the reported load-health picture, so ACWR bands should not be used as fixed training prescriptions.",
   "rtp":"Not applicable as a return-to-sport study. It reports health problems across a season, not return-to-play decisions, so it cannot be used to decide how quickly a returning player can increase training load."
 }
}

   "limitations":"Health problems were self-reported and not medically confirmed, 31% of daily questionnaires were unanswered, and the post-study survey found under-reporting. Several Discussion figures conflict with Table 2, including all health problems (31% in the table vs 33% in the abstract), new non-contact injuries (6% vs 2%), 28-day vs 21-day periods (15% vs 26% significant, the reverse of the text), and coupled vs non-coupled (21% vs 19%); table values are reported here. The text describes the strongest association as coupled 7:21 EWMA (OR 5.27), which does not match the figure, and the PDF prints no publication year, so 2020 comes from the Crossref record.",
   "practicalImplications":"Staff reading ACWR studies should ask whether all analyses were reported and how ACWR was calculated before trusting a single significant result. When collecting data for youth squads, the paper supports recording all health complaints, not only time-loss injuries, but it does not support using ACWR thresholds to manage load.",
   "athleteDev":"Limited. The study does not test whether ACWR-guided load changes improve performance. Its relevance is that calculation choices (period length, rolling average vs EWMA, categories) change the reported load-health picture, so ACWR bands should not be used as fixed training prescriptions.",
   "rtp":"Not applicable as a return-to-sport study. It reports health problems across a season, not return-to-play decisions, so it cannot be used to decide how quickly a returning player can increase training load."
 }
}
