1	A cherry tree ripe for picking: The relationship between the acute:chronic workload
2	ratio and health problems
3	Torstein Dalen-Lorentsen, MSc1
4	Thor Einar Andersen, PT, MD, PhD1
5	John Bjørneboe, MD, PhD1
6	Markus Vagle, MSc1,2
7	Kevin Nordanger Martin, PT, BSc1
8	Michael Kleppen, MSc1
9	Morten Wang Fagerland, PhD1,3
10	Benjamin Clarsen, PT, PhD1, 4
11	1
12	Oslo Sports Trauma Research Center, Department of Sports Medicine, Norwegian
13	School of Sports Sciences, Oslo.
14	Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®
15	2
16	Department of Sports, Physical Education and Outdoor Studies, University of South-
17	Eastern Norway, Horten.
18	3
19	Oslo Centre for Biostatistics and Epidemiology, Research Support Services, Oslo
20	University Hospital, Oslo.
21	4
22	Center for Disease Burden, Norwegian Institute of Public Health, Bergen.
23	This study protocol was approved by the South-Eastern Norway Regional Committee
24	for Medical and Health Research Ethics (2017/1015) and the Norwegian Centre for
25	Research Data (5487). We declare no conflict of interest or financial involvement in
26	any organization or entity with financial interest in the subject of matter discussed in
27	the article.
28	Address correspondence to Torstein Dalen-Lorentsen, Sognsveien 220, 0860 Oslo,
29	Norway, Torstein.dalen@nih.no
30	1
31	Copyright © ${year} Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®. All rights reserved.
32	ABSTRACT
33	2 Objective: To investigate whether the relationship between the acute:chronic
34	3 workload ratio (ACWR) and health problems varies when different methodological
35	4 approaches are used to quantify the relationship.
36	5 Design: Prospective cohort study
37	6 Methods: An online questionnaire was used to collect daily health and training
38	7 information from 86 elite youth footballers for 105 days. The relationship between
39	Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®
40	8 players’ training load and health was analysed using a range of different definitions of
41	9 ACWR and health problems. We used a 21-day and 28-day chronic period, coupled
42	10 and uncoupled calculations, and exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA)
43	11 and rolling average (RA). ACWR data were categorized into three bins (low, medium
44	12 and high) using pre-defined categories and z-scores, and we compared medium to
45	13 high, medium to low and low to high categories. The outcome was defined in three
46	14 ways: “all health problems”, “all injuries”, and “new non-contact injuries”. We
47	15 performed random-effects logistic regression analyses of all combinations, a total of
48	16 108 analyses.
49	17 Results We recorded 6250 training days and 196 health problems. Of the 108
50	Copyright © ${year} Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®. All rights reserved.
51	18 analyses performed, 24 (22%) identified a statistically significant (p<0.05) association
52	19 between ACWR and health problems. A greater proportion of significant associations
53	20 were identified when using an EWMA (42% of analyses), when comparing low and
54	21 high categories (33%), and using “all health problems” definition (33%).
55	22 Conclusions: The relationship between ACWR and health problems was dependent
56	23 on methodological approach.
57	24 Keywords: ACWR, Football, Injury, Training Load
58	2
59	25 INTRODUCTION
60	26 The acute:chronic workload ratio (ACWR) was introduced by Hulin and co-
61	27 workers in 201431 as a modification of Banister’s fitness-fatigue model 5. It is
62	28 calculated by dividing the total sum of all training an athlete has recently completed
63	29 (normally the previous week) by the sum they have completed over a longer period
64	30 (e.g., the previous 4 weeks). ACWR is intended to reflect athletes' preparedness for
65	31 training by accounting for both positive and negative training effects (i.e. fitness and
66	32 fatigue) 25. The relationship between ACWR and health problems has emerged as a
67	Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®
68	33 popular topic among practitioners and researchers alike; since 2014, at least 45
69	34 cohort studies and multiple reviews have addressed the topic (supplementary #1).
70	35 The quality of the evidence supporting ACWR has been questioned 36, and several
71	36 methodological aspects of ACWR calculation and analysis have been debated 11, 20,
72	30, 43, 44, 52, 60, 66, 71, 73
73	37 .
74	38 There is no consensus on how the relationship between ACWR and health
75	39 problems should be calculated and analysed, and no two studies have used the
76	40 same approach. Although most studies report significant findings (supplementary
77	41 #1), their results and conclusions are inconsistent, and few studies consider their
78	Copyright © ${year} Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®. All rights reserved.
79	42 negative findings when making conclusions. The inconsistent results among ACWR
80	43 studies may reflect differences in methodology, particularly (1) how training load and
81	44 health problems were recorded, (2) how ACWR was calculated, and (3) how the
82	45 relationship between ACWR and health problems was analysed.
83	46 We aimed to analyse the relationship between ACWR and health problems
84	47 among elite youth football players using a wide range of methodological
85	48 combinations defined before analysis. We considered the extent to which these
86	3
87	49 methodological choices influenced the relationship between ACWR and health
88	50 problems.
89	51 METHODS
90	52 We conducted a prospective cohort study from July to October 2017. During
91	53 this period, which included one-two weeks of summer break and 13-14 weeks of
92	54 regular in-season competition, players recorded their daily training load and health
93	Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®
94	55 status using an online survey software (Briteback AB, version 2.5.3.1; Norrköping,
95	56 Sweden). We obtained approval from the South-Eastern Norway Regional
96	57 Committee for Medical and Health Research Ethics (2017/1015) and the Norwegian
97	58 Centre for Research Data (5487) before study start. All participants or their guardians
98	59 provided written informed consent. Participants were not involved in the design,
99	60 conduct, interpretation, and/or translation of this paper.
100	61 Recruitment
101	62 We invited a convenience sample of 12 (six girls’ and six boys’ teams)
102	63 Norwegian football (soccer) teams from the elite U-19 divisions to participate. Teams
103	64 that already used a training load management system were excluded (n=6), as their
104	Copyright © ${year} Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®. All rights reserved.
105	65 data could potentially be non-comparable to previous studies. Six teams (3 girls’ and
106	66 3 boys’) accepted the invitation to participate in the study, and all players in these
107	67 teams agreed to participate. We invited all permanent squad members of these
108	68 teams, except players with existing health problems that we expected would render
109	69 them unavailable for football training and match play during the study period (as they
110	70 would not provide any data). No power or sample size calculation was performed
111	71 before the study.
112	4
113	72 Collection of training load data
114	73 Players reported their daily training load using a short online questionnaire
115	74 (supplementary file #2). A link to the questionnaire was distributed by an automated
116	75 short message service (SMS) at 9 p.m. every evening. If players had not replied to
117	76 the questionnaire before 8 a.m. the following morning, they received an SMS
118	77 reminder. The questionnaire included questions with structured response options on
119	78 training load data for all football activity, including organized training and matches, as
120	Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®
121	79 well as non-organized football play (supplementary #2). Players were asked to record
122	80 the duration in minutes and their overall perceived rate of physical exertion (RPE)
123	81 using the modified Borg CR-10 scale 23. We calculated an arbitrary training load unit
124	82 (AU) by multiplying the duration and the session RPE (sRPE) 23 for all football
125	83 activity.
126	84 Collection of health data
127	85 Players recorded their health status in the daily questionnaire by answering
128	86 two questions, (1) have you experienced a new health problem and, (2) have you
129	87 experienced a worsening of an existing health problem? Players were asked to report
130	88 all complaints, irrespective of their consequences on football participation or their
131	Copyright © ${year} Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®. All rights reserved.
132	89 need to seek medical attention 24. If the player reported any new health problems or a
133	90 worsening of an existing problem, a sports medicine clinician (physiotherapist or
134	91 chiropractor) contacted them by telephone the following day to conduct a structured
135	92 interview. During this interview, we classified health problems according to the Union
136	93 of European Football Associations (UEFA) guidelines as injury or illness, acute or
137	94 overuse, contact or non-contact, injury mechanism, tissue and body part
138	95 (supplementary #3) 34.
139	5
140	96 Efforts to limit potential sources of bias
141	97 We standardized sRPE-registration by collecting data at 9 p.m., when football
142	98 activity was likely to be finished, and when the player was unlikely to be in the
143	99 presence of their teammates. To maximize the likelihood of honest reports, we
144	100 assured players that all their training and health data would be treated as confidential
145	101 and not disclosed to their coach or teammates. Players were familiarised with the
146	102 RPE scale during information meetings before the study, and we instructed players to
147	Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®
148	103 consider the whole session when giving a RPE score. We contacted coaches weekly
149	104 to engage their support in motivating their players to respond to the questionnaire.
150	105 Any player who consistently failed to respond to the automated reminder-SMS was
151	106 sent personal messages to encourage them to resume participation. To ensure
152	107 consistent reporting of all health problems, we familiarized players with the definitions
153	108 in the pre-study meeting and emphasized the importance of reporting all health
154	109 problems, irrespective of their consequences.
155	110 The questionnaire has not been validated. At the time of data collection, there
156	111 were no validated alternatives. However, 10 players from the same population pilot
157	112 tested the questionnaire for three weeks and established a high face validity.
158	Copyright © ${year} Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®. All rights reserved.
159	113 To assess the potential bias in our results, we conducted an anonymous post-study
160	114 survey of all participants, asking whether the players had reported all training and
161	115 health data as instructed.
162	116 Variables
163	117 All independent (training load) and dependent (health status) variables were
164	118 defined a priori.
165	6
166	119 Independent variables
167	120 ACWR was calculated in eight different ways, using all combinations of the
168	121 following:
169	122 • The “acute” and “chronic” workload periods were defined in two ways: 7 to 28
170	123 days and 7 to 21 days.
171	124 • Training load was calculated for each period using a simple rolling average
172	125 (RA) and exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA; for formulas, see
173	Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®
174	126 supplementary file #4) 71.
175	127 • For RA calculations, we included the acute period in the chronic period
176	128 (coupled approach) and separated it from the chronic period (uncoupled
177	129 approach). As the original EWMA formula is coupled by nature71 and to limit
178	130 the number of analyses, no uncoupled approach was used.
179	131
180	132 ACWR variables were then converted into ordinal categorical variables with two
181	133 methods:
182	134 • Pre-defined bins using the most common categories: Low (<0.8), medium (0.8
183	Copyright © ${year} Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®. All rights reserved.
184	135 to 1.5) and high (>1.5)31, 39.
185	136 • Z-scores: Low (<1 standard deviation (SD) below the mean), medium (1 SD
186	137 below the mean to 1 SD above the mean), high (>1 SD above the mean).
187	138 o Z-score categories for RA was: Low (<0.4), medium (0.4 to 1.81) and
188	139 high (>1.81)
189	140 o Z-score categories for EWMA was: Low (<0.32), medium (0.32 to 1.73)
190	141 and high (>1.73)
191	7
192	142 Dependent variables
193	143 Using players’ daily health reports, we created three different dependent variables
194	144 for analysis:
195	145 • Any worsening in health status (yes/no): all new injuries and illnesses, and all
196	146 cases when players reported a worsening of an existing injury or illness
197	147 • Any worsening in injury status (yes/no): all new injuries and cases when
198	148 players reported a worsening of an existing injury. Illnesses were excluded.
199	Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®
200	149 • Any new non-contact injury (yes/no)
201	150 Statistical analyses
202	151 All statistical methods were defined before analysis. A random-effects logistic
203	152 regression model was used to investigate all combinations of the 12 independent and
204	153 3 dependent variables, comparing the medium ACWR group to the low and high
205	154 groups, and the low group to the high group. We performed a total of 108 (all
206	155 combinations X comparisons) separate analyses using Stata software (version 15.3
207	156 StataCorp LLC, College Station, TX), with the xtlogit command (see supplementary
208	157 file #5 for script). A random-intercept model was used, and the random error term
209	Copyright © ${year} Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®. All rights reserved.
210	158 was assumed normal distributed (with mean 0). We did not adjust the regression
211	159 models for confounding by sex, age or for the effect of clustering by individuals and
212	160 teams. However, the adjusted analyses are available as supplementary material (#5).
213	161 The incidence rate was calculated by dividing the total number of cases satisfying
214	162 each health problem definition by the total exposure time and multiplying by 1000
215	163 hours. We calculated the absolute daily risk of health problems by dividing the
216	164 number of cases satisfying each health problem definition by the total number of
217	165 athlete days in the study.
218	8
219	166 Missing data
220	167 When athletes’ training load data were incomplete, either due to missing
221	168 session duration or RPE, we replaced the missing values of individual players with
222	169 the team average for that session. If an entire session was unreported, we did not
223	170 attempt to estimate missing data. Instead, we defined a minimum amount of
224	171 information necessary to make an ACWR calculation (5 days for a 7-day acute
225	172 period, 14 days for a 21-day chronic period and 21 days for a 28-day chronic period)
226	Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®
227	173 and used a statistical model (random-effects logistic regression) capable of handling
228	174 incomplete datasets.
229	175 RESULTS
230	176 A total of 86 players agreed to participate, 47 males (mean age 17.5, SD 0.7),
231	177 and 39 females (mean age 17.5, SD 1.3). The overall response to the daily
232	178 questionnaire was 69% (6250 of 9030 athlete days).
233	179 Training load and exposure
234	180 The median weekly training load per player was 1262 AU (interquartile range;
235	181 IQR [1024, 1422]) for training and 439 AU [425, 536] for matches. The total exposure
236	Copyright © ${year} Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®. All rights reserved.
237	182 during the study, including both training and matches, was 4668 hours. The median
238	183 weekly exposure was 242 [155, 329] training minutes and 64 [47, 81] match minutes,
239	184 a total of 306 minutes [274, 338] per player.
240	185 Health problems
241	186 Insert table 1 about here
242	187 A total of 196 health problems were reported. Of these, 91 were classified as
243	188 injuries, 17 as illness, and 88 were not classified. During the study period, 65 players
244	9
245	189 (75% of all players) reported a health problem, 62 players (72%) registered an injury,
246	190 and 39 (45%) reported a new non-contact injury. The incidence rate and daily risk of
247	191 health problems are shown in Table 1.
248	192 Insert table 2 about here
249	193 Main results: Association between ACWR and health problems
250	194 Of the 108 analyses performed, we found 24 (22%) significant associations
251	Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®
252	195 between ACWR and health problems, spread across various methodological
253	196 combinations (figure 1). We did not observe any patterns of combinations that
254	197 substantially increased the chance of a significant association. The single most
255	198 frequent component among the significant combinations was EWMA with 15 of the
256	199 24 significant associations. The strongest association observed was with the
257	200 following combination: a coupled 7-day acute, 21-day chronic time-period using
258	201 EWMA, and by pre-defined categories comparing low to high category with all
259	202 injuries as health problem definition (OR: 5.27 95% CI: 1.83-15.24).
260	203 Insert figure 1 about here
261	Copyright © ${year} Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®. All rights reserved.
262	204 Post-study survey
263	205 Forty-five players (53%) responded to the post-study survey. Of these, 15
264	206 (33%) players said they had not reported training load data every day as instructed.
265	207 Participants described the two main reasons why they did not report training load
266	208 data: (1) they had forgotten to reply to the SMS (9 players), and (2) that it was too
267	209 time-consuming (two players). Thirteen players (29%) admitted they had not reported
268	210 all health problems, with the most frequent explanations that they did not think the
269	10
270	211 problem was significant enough (eight players) and that they did not want to be
271	212 contacted by phone for the follow-up interview (three players).
272	213 DISCUSSION
273	214 We aimed to explore the effect on different methodological choices on the
274	215 association between ACWR and health problems. As this was a critique of current
275	216 methods in ACWR research, we based our choice of methods on the published
276	Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®
277	217 literature and do not necessarily endorse their future use. We analysed 108 different
278	218 methodological combinations and found 24 (22%) significant associations between
279	219 ACWR and health problems. There was a large variation in the size and precision of
280	220 the estimated strength of the association. Our main conclusion is that the potential
281	221 association between ACWR and health problems is affected by methodological
282	222 choices.
283	223 Health problem definition
284	224 The definition of a health problem had the largest effect on the number of
285	225 significant associations identified between ACWR and health problems. When
286	226 analysed with the broadest definition, almost one in three analyses was significant,
287	Copyright © ${year} Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®. All rights reserved.
288	227 but when using the narrower definitions all injuries and new non-contact injuries, the
289	228 proportion of significant findings was reduced (25% and 2% respectively). One likely
290	229 explanation is that the number of cases was reduced from 196 to 45 when we
291	230 applied the most narrow health problem definition. This is likely to be too few cases
292	231 to detect a small to moderate association (which requires approximately 200 cases)
293	4
294	232 . As only six out of the 43 studies that provided number of cases (supplementary #1)
295	11
296	233 included more than 200, a large proportion of studies in this field appear to be
297	234 underpowered.
298	235 Most ACWR studies have used a time-loss health problems definition 7-9, 15, 17-19, 21, 22,
299	29, 31, 32, 38, 40, 41, 45-48, 50, 54, 55, 57, 58, 61-64, 67, 68, 74
300	236 . However, the narrow definition is
301	237 unlikely to capture a majority of overuse injuries, which do not often lead to time loss
302	3, 13, 14
303	238 . As overuse injuries are likely the injury type most associated with training
304	239 load, we believe it is essential to use a broad health problems definition in future
305	Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®
306	240 training load studies.12, 13
307	241 ACWR calculation
308	242 The duration of the acute and chronic time-periods varies considerably
309	243 between the previous ACWR studies. Time-periods are often sport-specific and
310	244 typically aim to represent one training micro-cycle (acute) and one macro-cycle
311	245 (chronic)10. We chose the two most used chronic periods, 28 days and 21 days and
312	246 found that 28 days had 50% more significant associations than 21. Most studies
313	247 define the acute period as 7 days (supplementary #1); however, some define it
314	248 differently (e.g. 3 day)1, 10. We did not investigate different acute period durations to
315	Copyright © ${year} Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®. All rights reserved.
316	249 limit the number of analyses.
317	250 Typically the average acute and chronic workloads are determined using a simple
318	251 rolling average of the entire period 7-9, 16-19, 21, 22, 29, 31-33, 37, 39-42, 45-47, 51, 53, 55-59, 61, 63-65,
319	67-69, 74
320	252 . However, Williams et al.71 proposed the use of an EWMA, whereby each
321	253 day’s contribution to the aggregate is exponentially greater than the previous day.
322	254 Several studies have shown EWMA-based ACWR calculations to be more closely
323	255 associated with health problems than RA-based calculations 21, 27, 39, 55, 62. Our
324	256 findings support this, with EWMA being significant in 42% of the analyses.
325	12
326	257 Recently, Lolli et al.43, 44 criticized the use of coupled ACWR, as it by definition leads
327	258 to a correlation between the numerator and the denominator in the ratio. We found
328	259 almost 50% more significant associations when using a coupled ACWR than non-
329	260 coupled, suggesting that the two cannot be directly compared.
330	261 ACWR analysis
331	262 Almost all training load data are converted from a continuous to a categorical
332	263 variable for analysis. Recently, Carey et al. highlighted problems with large false
333	Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®
334	264 discovery and rejection rates with this approach 11. Loss of power and residual
335	265 confounding are other important problems with discretization of continuous variables
336	2, 6
337	266 , and cannot be recommended in ACWR research. Despite the challenges, few
338	267 attempts have been made to investigate ACWR as a continuous variable 41 . Instead,
339	268 studies have categorised ACWR values according to the first ACWR publication 31, or
340	269 by z scores. We categorised data in two ways, using pre-defined cut-off values and
341	270 using a z-score, and there was not a large difference between the two. Rather, the
342	271 limitations of each approach should be recognised. In small sample sizes, or in any
343	272 sample size that discretises into small brackets, sparse data is likely to affect
344	273 results,26, 66 and especially in the low-categories where data are likely to be limited.
345	Copyright © ${year} Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®. All rights reserved.
346	274 This is apparent in our results when considering the inconsistency in the OR
347	275 estimates particularly in the comparisons that included the low category. The analysis
348	276 of categories with low power provides uncertainty and should be interpreted with
349	277 caution.
350	278 Another consideration with discretizing is the number of categories and the
351	279 comparison between these. The number of categories and comparisons vary across
352	280 the literature (supplementary #1). We chose to compare a medium category to high
353	13
354	281 and low, and the low category to high. In both cases involving an increased ACWR
355	282 we found significantly higher odds of developing a health problem in almost 1 in 3
356	283 analyses. In contrast, we only identified two significant associations when comparing
357	284 medium to low ACWR. This finding contrasts with the originally-described ACWR
358	285 concept, which suggested an increased injury risk when ACWR was low 25. We note
359	286 that few (n=2) 63, 69 other studies have supported this aspect of the concept, and
360	287 question its biological rationale.
361	Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®
362	288 We believe that discretisation is inappropriate in ACWR-injury studies and a method
363	289 for modeling training load as a continuous variable is warranted.
364	290 Statistical approach
365	291 A variety of statistical models have been used to analyse the workload
366	292 between ACWR and health problems. Most studies have used an overly-simple
367	293 approach, without accounting for the multifactorial aetiology of injuries, between-
368	294 athlete or within-athlete assessments, missing and unbalanced data, and the nature
369	295 of time-varying variables 72. To tackle some of these challenges, we chose a random-
370	296 effects logistic regression model, which is one of two recommended approaches 72.
371	Copyright © ${year} Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®. All rights reserved.
372	297 Nevertheless, we believe that research comparing the results of different statistical
373	298 approaches is warranted.
374	299 Methodological considerations
375	300 We collected health data directly from athletes; a design that has not
376	301 previously been used in ACWR studies. This approach allowed us to use a broad
377	302 definition of health problems, which means we are likely to have captured a far
378	303 greater proportion of overuse injuries than previous studies 12, 13. However, this
379	14
380	304 approach also has limitations. Health problems were not medically confirmed, lacked
381	305 diagnostic details, and in many cases were not fully classified (e.g. as acute or
382	306 overuse injuries). Furthermore, players failed to respond to 31% of the daily
383	307 questionnaires and, as illustrated by our post-study survey, did not always report
384	308 every health problem or training session, potentially leading to selection bias.
385	309 Session-RPE is considered a validated method for measuring training load across
386	310 various sports 28, and for elite youth footballers specifically 35. We chose sRPE
387	Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®
388	311 because it was the most practical way to quantify load in footballers of this level and
389	312 because a large majority of previous ACWR studies have used it as their primary
390	313 load measure.
391	314 The handling of missing data might affect our results, and we used a sub-optimal
392	315 method where the team average replaced missing values when either duration or
393	316 RPE were missing. Although this is the most common method used in previous
394	317 studies, future research should investigate better options, such as the methods
395	318 discussed in White et al70. We cannot exclude the possibility that the discretization of
396	319 ACWR has influenced results through a loss of data, false discovery and rejection
397	320 rates, residual confounding and sparse data bias 26.
398	Copyright © ${year} Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®. All rights reserved.
399	321 Future directions
400	322 All previous ACWR studies have used different methodological approaches and their
401	323 findings are inconsistent. In general, the conclusions of these studies have focussed
402	324 on significant findings. We have demonstrated the number of non-significant findings
403	325 likely to be behind every positive one. Reporting bias is therefore an important
404	326 consideration when assessing the overall evidence for the relationship between
405	15
406	327 ACWR and health problems. Although each sport and study population are different,
407	328 methodological consensus for workload studies is needed.
408	329 Finally, we question the need for more underpowered risk factor studies examining
409	330 the relationship between training load and health problems. We believe that to
410	331 improve our understanding of the relationship between ACWR and health problems;
411	332 it is necessary to conduct much larger observational studies (i.e. thousands and not
412	333 hundreds of injuries), as well as experimental research such as randomised
413	Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®
414	334 controlled trials.
415	335 Conclusion
416	336 The potential association between ACWR and health problems is affected by
417	337 methodological choices. Future ACWR studies should pre-register their definitions,
418	338 hypotheses and models, and report the results of all performed analyses.
419	339 KEY POINTS
420	340 Findings
421	341 The relationship between ACWR and health problems depends on
422	Copyright © ${year} Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®. All rights reserved.
423	342 methodological choices.
424	343 If investigators cherry-pick positive results (i.e. only report significant findings,
425	344 rather than the results of all analyses) an overestimation of the association between
426	345 ACWR and health problems is expected.
427	346 Implications
428	16
429	347 In future studies of training load and health problems, we encourage
430	348 researchers to report all analyses performed, as well as their rationale for all
431	349 methodological choices.
432	350 Different study designs are needed to test whether using ACWR to manage
433	351 athletes’ training load is an effective injury prevention measure.
434	352 Practitioners should be cautious when comparing studies using different
435	353 methodological approach and be aware the possibility that authors may choose to
436	Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®
437	354 report only the results that support their own hypotheses.
438	355 Caution
439	356 A limitation of this study is the use of sub-optimal methods from previously
440	357 published articles. This was done to compare the difference of previous approaches.
441	358 We did not intend the results to be interpreted to evidence for the relationship
442	359 between ACWR and health problem itself.

A cherry tree ripe for picking: The relationship between the acute:chronic workload
ratio and health problems
Torstein Dalen-Lorentsen, MSc1
Thor Einar Andersen, PT, MD, PhD1
John Bjørneboe, MD, PhD1
Markus Vagle, MSc1,2
Kevin Nordanger Martin, PT, BSc1
Michael Kleppen, MSc1
Morten Wang Fagerland, PhD1,3
Benjamin Clarsen, PT, PhD1, 4
1
Oslo Sports Trauma Research Center, Department of Sports Medicine, Norwegian
School of Sports Sciences, Oslo.
Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®
2
Department of Sports, Physical Education and Outdoor Studies, University of South-
Eastern Norway, Horten.
3
Oslo Centre for Biostatistics and Epidemiology, Research Support Services, Oslo
University Hospital, Oslo.
4
Center for Disease Burden, Norwegian Institute of Public Health, Bergen.
This study protocol was approved by the South-Eastern Norway Regional Committee
for Medical and Health Research Ethics (2017/1015) and the Norwegian Centre for
Research Data (5487). We declare no conflict of interest or financial involvement in
any organization or entity with financial interest in the subject of matter discussed in
the article.
Address correspondence to Torstein Dalen-Lorentsen, Sognsveien 220, 0860 Oslo,
Norway, Torstein.dalen@nih.no
1
Copyright © ${year} Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®. All rights reserved.
ABSTRACT
2 Objective: To investigate whether the relationship between the acute:chronic
3 workload ratio (ACWR) and health problems varies when different methodological
4 approaches are used to quantify the relationship.
5 Design: Prospective cohort study
6 Methods: An online questionnaire was used to collect daily health and training
7 information from 86 elite youth footballers for 105 days. The relationship between
Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®
8 players’ training load and health was analysed using a range of different definitions of
9 ACWR and health problems. We used a 21-day and 28-day chronic period, coupled
10 and uncoupled calculations, and exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA)
11 and rolling average (RA). ACWR data were categorized into three bins (low, medium
12 and high) using pre-defined categories and z-scores, and we compared medium to
13 high, medium to low and low to high categories. The outcome was defined in three
14 ways: “all health problems”, “all injuries”, and “new non-contact injuries”. We
15 performed random-effects logistic regression analyses of all combinations, a total of
16 108 analyses.
17 Results We recorded 6250 training days and 196 health problems. Of the 108
Copyright © ${year} Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®. All rights reserved.
18 analyses performed, 24 (22%) identified a statistically significant (p<0.05) association
19 between ACWR and health problems. A greater proportion of significant associations
20 were identified when using an EWMA (42% of analyses), when comparing low and
21 high categories (33%), and using “all health problems” definition (33%).
22 Conclusions: The relationship between ACWR and health problems was dependent
23 on methodological approach.
24 Keywords: ACWR, Football, Injury, Training Load
2
25 INTRODUCTION
26 The acute:chronic workload ratio (ACWR) was introduced by Hulin and co-
27 workers in 201431 as a modification of Banister’s fitness-fatigue model 5. It is
28 calculated by dividing the total sum of all training an athlete has recently completed
29 (normally the previous week) by the sum they have completed over a longer period
30 (e.g., the previous 4 weeks). ACWR is intended to reflect athletes' preparedness for
31 training by accounting for both positive and negative training effects (i.e. fitness and
32 fatigue) 25. The relationship between ACWR and health problems has emerged as a
Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®
33 popular topic among practitioners and researchers alike; since 2014, at least 45
34 cohort studies and multiple reviews have addressed the topic (supplementary #1).
35 The quality of the evidence supporting ACWR has been questioned 36, and several
36 methodological aspects of ACWR calculation and analysis have been debated 11, 20,
30, 43, 44, 52, 60, 66, 71, 73
37 .
38 There is no consensus on how the relationship between ACWR and health
39 problems should be calculated and analysed, and no two studies have used the
40 same approach. Although most studies report significant findings (supplementary
41 #1), their results and conclusions are inconsistent, and few studies consider their
Copyright © ${year} Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®. All rights reserved.
42 negative findings when making conclusions. The inconsistent results among ACWR
43 studies may reflect differences in methodology, particularly (1) how training load and
44 health problems were recorded, (2) how ACWR was calculated, and (3) how the
45 relationship between ACWR and health problems was analysed.
46 We aimed to analyse the relationship between ACWR and health problems
47 among elite youth football players using a wide range of methodological
48 combinations defined before analysis. We considered the extent to which these
3
49 methodological choices influenced the relationship between ACWR and health
50 problems.
51 METHODS
52 We conducted a prospective cohort study from July to October 2017. During
53 this period, which included one-two weeks of summer break and 13-14 weeks of
54 regular in-season competition, players recorded their daily training load and health
Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®
55 status using an online survey software (Briteback AB, version 2.5.3.1; Norrköping,
56 Sweden). We obtained approval from the South-Eastern Norway Regional
57 Committee for Medical and Health Research Ethics (2017/1015) and the Norwegian
58 Centre for Research Data (5487) before study start. All participants or their guardians
59 provided written informed consent. Participants were not involved in the design,
60 conduct, interpretation, and/or translation of this paper.
61 Recruitment
62 We invited a convenience sample of 12 (six girls’ and six boys’ teams)
63 Norwegian football (soccer) teams from the elite U-19 divisions to participate. Teams
64 that already used a training load management system were excluded (n=6), as their
Copyright © ${year} Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®. All rights reserved.
65 data could potentially be non-comparable to previous studies. Six teams (3 girls’ and
66 3 boys’) accepted the invitation to participate in the study, and all players in these
67 teams agreed to participate. We invited all permanent squad members of these
68 teams, except players with existing health problems that we expected would render
69 them unavailable for football training and match play during the study period (as they
70 would not provide any data). No power or sample size calculation was performed
71 before the study.
4
72 Collection of training load data
73 Players reported their daily training load using a short online questionnaire
74 (supplementary file #2). A link to the questionnaire was distributed by an automated
75 short message service (SMS) at 9 p.m. every evening. If players had not replied to
76 the questionnaire before 8 a.m. the following morning, they received an SMS
77 reminder. The questionnaire included questions with structured response options on
78 training load data for all football activity, including organized training and matches, as
Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®
79 well as non-organized football play (supplementary #2). Players were asked to record
80 the duration in minutes and their overall perceived rate of physical exertion (RPE)
81 using the modified Borg CR-10 scale 23. We calculated an arbitrary training load unit
82 (AU) by multiplying the duration and the session RPE (sRPE) 23 for all football
83 activity.
84 Collection of health data
85 Players recorded their health status in the daily questionnaire by answering
86 two questions, (1) have you experienced a new health problem and, (2) have you
87 experienced a worsening of an existing health problem? Players were asked to report
88 all complaints, irrespective of their consequences on football participation or their
Copyright © ${year} Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®. All rights reserved.
89 need to seek medical attention 24. If the player reported any new health problems or a
90 worsening of an existing problem, a sports medicine clinician (physiotherapist or
91 chiropractor) contacted them by telephone the following day to conduct a structured
92 interview. During this interview, we classified health problems according to the Union
93 of European Football Associations (UEFA) guidelines as injury or illness, acute or
94 overuse, contact or non-contact, injury mechanism, tissue and body part
95 (supplementary #3) 34.
5
96 Efforts to limit potential sources of bias
97 We standardized sRPE-registration by collecting data at 9 p.m., when football
98 activity was likely to be finished, and when the player was unlikely to be in the
99 presence of their teammates. To maximize the likelihood of honest reports, we
100 assured players that all their training and health data would be treated as confidential
101 and not disclosed to their coach or teammates. Players were familiarised with the
102 RPE scale during information meetings before the study, and we instructed players to
Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®
103 consider the whole session when giving a RPE score. We contacted coaches weekly
104 to engage their support in motivating their players to respond to the questionnaire.
105 Any player who consistently failed to respond to the automated reminder-SMS was
106 sent personal messages to encourage them to resume participation. To ensure
107 consistent reporting of all health problems, we familiarized players with the definitions
108 in the pre-study meeting and emphasized the importance of reporting all health
109 problems, irrespective of their consequences.
110 The questionnaire has not been validated. At the time of data collection, there
111 were no validated alternatives. However, 10 players from the same population pilot
112 tested the questionnaire for three weeks and established a high face validity.
Copyright © ${year} Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®. All rights reserved.
113 To assess the potential bias in our results, we conducted an anonymous post-study
114 survey of all participants, asking whether the players had reported all training and
115 health data as instructed.
116 Variables
117 All independent (training load) and dependent (health status) variables were
118 defined a priori.
6
119 Independent variables
120 ACWR was calculated in eight different ways, using all combinations of the
121 following:
122 • The “acute” and “chronic” workload periods were defined in two ways: 7 to 28
123 days and 7 to 21 days.
124 • Training load was calculated for each period using a simple rolling average
125 (RA) and exponentially weighted moving average (EWMA; for formulas, see
Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®
126 supplementary file #4) 71.
127 • For RA calculations, we included the acute period in the chronic period
128 (coupled approach) and separated it from the chronic period (uncoupled
129 approach). As the original EWMA formula is coupled by nature71 and to limit
130 the number of analyses, no uncoupled approach was used.
131
132 ACWR variables were then converted into ordinal categorical variables with two
133 methods:
134 • Pre-defined bins using the most common categories: Low (<0.8), medium (0.8
Copyright © ${year} Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®. All rights reserved.
135 to 1.5) and high (>1.5)31, 39.
136 • Z-scores: Low (<1 standard deviation (SD) below the mean), medium (1 SD
137 below the mean to 1 SD above the mean), high (>1 SD above the mean).
138 o Z-score categories for RA was: Low (<0.4), medium (0.4 to 1.81) and
139 high (>1.81)
140 o Z-score categories for EWMA was: Low (<0.32), medium (0.32 to 1.73)
141 and high (>1.73)
7
142 Dependent variables
143 Using players’ daily health reports, we created three different dependent variables
144 for analysis:
145 • Any worsening in health status (yes/no): all new injuries and illnesses, and all
146 cases when players reported a worsening of an existing injury or illness
147 • Any worsening in injury status (yes/no): all new injuries and cases when
148 players reported a worsening of an existing injury. Illnesses were excluded.
Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®
149 • Any new non-contact injury (yes/no)
150 Statistical analyses
151 All statistical methods were defined before analysis. A random-effects logistic
152 regression model was used to investigate all combinations of the 12 independent and
153 3 dependent variables, comparing the medium ACWR group to the low and high
154 groups, and the low group to the high group. We performed a total of 108 (all
155 combinations X comparisons) separate analyses using Stata software (version 15.3
156 StataCorp LLC, College Station, TX), with the xtlogit command (see supplementary
157 file #5 for script). A random-intercept model was used, and the random error term
Copyright © ${year} Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®. All rights reserved.
158 was assumed normal distributed (with mean 0). We did not adjust the regression
159 models for confounding by sex, age or for the effect of clustering by individuals and
160 teams. However, the adjusted analyses are available as supplementary material (#5).
161 The incidence rate was calculated by dividing the total number of cases satisfying
162 each health problem definition by the total exposure time and multiplying by 1000
163 hours. We calculated the absolute daily risk of health problems by dividing the
164 number of cases satisfying each health problem definition by the total number of
165 athlete days in the study.
8
166 Missing data
167 When athletes’ training load data were incomplete, either due to missing
168 session duration or RPE, we replaced the missing values of individual players with
169 the team average for that session. If an entire session was unreported, we did not
170 attempt to estimate missing data. Instead, we defined a minimum amount of
171 information necessary to make an ACWR calculation (5 days for a 7-day acute
172 period, 14 days for a 21-day chronic period and 21 days for a 28-day chronic period)
Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®
173 and used a statistical model (random-effects logistic regression) capable of handling
174 incomplete datasets.
175 RESULTS
176 A total of 86 players agreed to participate, 47 males (mean age 17.5, SD 0.7),
177 and 39 females (mean age 17.5, SD 1.3). The overall response to the daily
178 questionnaire was 69% (6250 of 9030 athlete days).
179 Training load and exposure
180 The median weekly training load per player was 1262 AU (interquartile range;
181 IQR [1024, 1422]) for training and 439 AU [425, 536] for matches. The total exposure
Copyright © ${year} Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®. All rights reserved.
182 during the study, including both training and matches, was 4668 hours. The median
183 weekly exposure was 242 [155, 329] training minutes and 64 [47, 81] match minutes,
184 a total of 306 minutes [274, 338] per player.
185 Health problems
186 Insert table 1 about here
187 A total of 196 health problems were reported. Of these, 91 were classified as
188 injuries, 17 as illness, and 88 were not classified. During the study period, 65 players
9
189 (75% of all players) reported a health problem, 62 players (72%) registered an injury,
190 and 39 (45%) reported a new non-contact injury. The incidence rate and daily risk of
191 health problems are shown in Table 1.
192 Insert table 2 about here
193 Main results: Association between ACWR and health problems
194 Of the 108 analyses performed, we found 24 (22%) significant associations
Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®
195 between ACWR and health problems, spread across various methodological
196 combinations (figure 1). We did not observe any patterns of combinations that
197 substantially increased the chance of a significant association. The single most
198 frequent component among the significant combinations was EWMA with 15 of the
199 24 significant associations. The strongest association observed was with the
200 following combination: a coupled 7-day acute, 21-day chronic time-period using
201 EWMA, and by pre-defined categories comparing low to high category with all
202 injuries as health problem definition (OR: 5.27 95% CI: 1.83-15.24).
203 Insert figure 1 about here
Copyright © ${year} Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®. All rights reserved.
204 Post-study survey
205 Forty-five players (53%) responded to the post-study survey. Of these, 15
206 (33%) players said they had not reported training load data every day as instructed.
207 Participants described the two main reasons why they did not report training load
208 data: (1) they had forgotten to reply to the SMS (9 players), and (2) that it was too
209 time-consuming (two players). Thirteen players (29%) admitted they had not reported
210 all health problems, with the most frequent explanations that they did not think the
10
211 problem was significant enough (eight players) and that they did not want to be
212 contacted by phone for the follow-up interview (three players).
213 DISCUSSION
214 We aimed to explore the effect on different methodological choices on the
215 association between ACWR and health problems. As this was a critique of current
216 methods in ACWR research, we based our choice of methods on the published
Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®
217 literature and do not necessarily endorse their future use. We analysed 108 different
218 methodological combinations and found 24 (22%) significant associations between
219 ACWR and health problems. There was a large variation in the size and precision of
220 the estimated strength of the association. Our main conclusion is that the potential
221 association between ACWR and health problems is affected by methodological
222 choices.
223 Health problem definition
224 The definition of a health problem had the largest effect on the number of
225 significant associations identified between ACWR and health problems. When
226 analysed with the broadest definition, almost one in three analyses was significant,
Copyright © ${year} Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®. All rights reserved.
227 but when using the narrower definitions all injuries and new non-contact injuries, the
228 proportion of significant findings was reduced (25% and 2% respectively). One likely
229 explanation is that the number of cases was reduced from 196 to 45 when we
230 applied the most narrow health problem definition. This is likely to be too few cases
231 to detect a small to moderate association (which requires approximately 200 cases)
4
232 . As only six out of the 43 studies that provided number of cases (supplementary #1)
11
233 included more than 200, a large proportion of studies in this field appear to be
234 underpowered.
235 Most ACWR studies have used a time-loss health problems definition 7-9, 15, 17-19, 21, 22,
29, 31, 32, 38, 40, 41, 45-48, 50, 54, 55, 57, 58, 61-64, 67, 68, 74
236 . However, the narrow definition is
237 unlikely to capture a majority of overuse injuries, which do not often lead to time loss
3, 13, 14
238 . As overuse injuries are likely the injury type most associated with training
239 load, we believe it is essential to use a broad health problems definition in future
Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®
240 training load studies.12, 13
241 ACWR calculation
242 The duration of the acute and chronic time-periods varies considerably
243 between the previous ACWR studies. Time-periods are often sport-specific and
244 typically aim to represent one training micro-cycle (acute) and one macro-cycle
245 (chronic)10. We chose the two most used chronic periods, 28 days and 21 days and
246 found that 28 days had 50% more significant associations than 21. Most studies
247 define the acute period as 7 days (supplementary #1); however, some define it
248 differently (e.g. 3 day)1, 10. We did not investigate different acute period durations to
Copyright © ${year} Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®. All rights reserved.
249 limit the number of analyses.
250 Typically the average acute and chronic workloads are determined using a simple
251 rolling average of the entire period 7-9, 16-19, 21, 22, 29, 31-33, 37, 39-42, 45-47, 51, 53, 55-59, 61, 63-65,
67-69, 74
252 . However, Williams et al.71 proposed the use of an EWMA, whereby each
253 day’s contribution to the aggregate is exponentially greater than the previous day.
254 Several studies have shown EWMA-based ACWR calculations to be more closely
255 associated with health problems than RA-based calculations 21, 27, 39, 55, 62. Our
256 findings support this, with EWMA being significant in 42% of the analyses.
12
257 Recently, Lolli et al.43, 44 criticized the use of coupled ACWR, as it by definition leads
258 to a correlation between the numerator and the denominator in the ratio. We found
259 almost 50% more significant associations when using a coupled ACWR than non-
260 coupled, suggesting that the two cannot be directly compared.
261 ACWR analysis
262 Almost all training load data are converted from a continuous to a categorical
263 variable for analysis. Recently, Carey et al. highlighted problems with large false
Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®
264 discovery and rejection rates with this approach 11. Loss of power and residual
265 confounding are other important problems with discretization of continuous variables
2, 6
266 , and cannot be recommended in ACWR research. Despite the challenges, few
267 attempts have been made to investigate ACWR as a continuous variable 41 . Instead,
268 studies have categorised ACWR values according to the first ACWR publication 31, or
269 by z scores. We categorised data in two ways, using pre-defined cut-off values and
270 using a z-score, and there was not a large difference between the two. Rather, the
271 limitations of each approach should be recognised. In small sample sizes, or in any
272 sample size that discretises into small brackets, sparse data is likely to affect
273 results,26, 66 and especially in the low-categories where data are likely to be limited.
Copyright © ${year} Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®. All rights reserved.
274 This is apparent in our results when considering the inconsistency in the OR
275 estimates particularly in the comparisons that included the low category. The analysis
276 of categories with low power provides uncertainty and should be interpreted with
277 caution.
278 Another consideration with discretizing is the number of categories and the
279 comparison between these. The number of categories and comparisons vary across
280 the literature (supplementary #1). We chose to compare a medium category to high
13
281 and low, and the low category to high. In both cases involving an increased ACWR
282 we found significantly higher odds of developing a health problem in almost 1 in 3
283 analyses. In contrast, we only identified two significant associations when comparing
284 medium to low ACWR. This finding contrasts with the originally-described ACWR
285 concept, which suggested an increased injury risk when ACWR was low 25. We note
286 that few (n=2) 63, 69 other studies have supported this aspect of the concept, and
287 question its biological rationale.
Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®
288 We believe that discretisation is inappropriate in ACWR-injury studies and a method
289 for modeling training load as a continuous variable is warranted.
290 Statistical approach
291 A variety of statistical models have been used to analyse the workload
292 between ACWR and health problems. Most studies have used an overly-simple
293 approach, without accounting for the multifactorial aetiology of injuries, between-
294 athlete or within-athlete assessments, missing and unbalanced data, and the nature
295 of time-varying variables 72. To tackle some of these challenges, we chose a random-
296 effects logistic regression model, which is one of two recommended approaches 72.
Copyright © ${year} Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®. All rights reserved.
297 Nevertheless, we believe that research comparing the results of different statistical
298 approaches is warranted.
299 Methodological considerations
300 We collected health data directly from athletes; a design that has not
301 previously been used in ACWR studies. This approach allowed us to use a broad
302 definition of health problems, which means we are likely to have captured a far
303 greater proportion of overuse injuries than previous studies 12, 13. However, this
14
304 approach also has limitations. Health problems were not medically confirmed, lacked
305 diagnostic details, and in many cases were not fully classified (e.g. as acute or
306 overuse injuries). Furthermore, players failed to respond to 31% of the daily
307 questionnaires and, as illustrated by our post-study survey, did not always report
308 every health problem or training session, potentially leading to selection bias.
309 Session-RPE is considered a validated method for measuring training load across
310 various sports 28, and for elite youth footballers specifically 35. We chose sRPE
Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®
311 because it was the most practical way to quantify load in footballers of this level and
312 because a large majority of previous ACWR studies have used it as their primary
313 load measure.
314 The handling of missing data might affect our results, and we used a sub-optimal
315 method where the team average replaced missing values when either duration or
316 RPE were missing. Although this is the most common method used in previous
317 studies, future research should investigate better options, such as the methods
318 discussed in White et al70. We cannot exclude the possibility that the discretization of
319 ACWR has influenced results through a loss of data, false discovery and rejection
320 rates, residual confounding and sparse data bias 26.
Copyright © ${year} Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®. All rights reserved.
321 Future directions
322 All previous ACWR studies have used different methodological approaches and their
323 findings are inconsistent. In general, the conclusions of these studies have focussed
324 on significant findings. We have demonstrated the number of non-significant findings
325 likely to be behind every positive one. Reporting bias is therefore an important
326 consideration when assessing the overall evidence for the relationship between
15
327 ACWR and health problems. Although each sport and study population are different,
328 methodological consensus for workload studies is needed.
329 Finally, we question the need for more underpowered risk factor studies examining
330 the relationship between training load and health problems. We believe that to
331 improve our understanding of the relationship between ACWR and health problems;
332 it is necessary to conduct much larger observational studies (i.e. thousands and not
333 hundreds of injuries), as well as experimental research such as randomised
Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®
334 controlled trials.
335 Conclusion
336 The potential association between ACWR and health problems is affected by
337 methodological choices. Future ACWR studies should pre-register their definitions,
338 hypotheses and models, and report the results of all performed analyses.
339 KEY POINTS
340 Findings
341 The relationship between ACWR and health problems depends on
Copyright © ${year} Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®. All rights reserved.
342 methodological choices.
343 If investigators cherry-pick positive results (i.e. only report significant findings,
344 rather than the results of all analyses) an overestimation of the association between
345 ACWR and health problems is expected.
346 Implications
16
347 In future studies of training load and health problems, we encourage
348 researchers to report all analyses performed, as well as their rationale for all
349 methodological choices.
350 Different study designs are needed to test whether using ACWR to manage
351 athletes’ training load is an effective injury prevention measure.
352 Practitioners should be cautious when comparing studies using different
353 methodological approach and be aware the possibility that authors may choose to
Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®
354 report only the results that support their own hypotheses.
355 Caution
356 A limitation of this study is the use of sub-optimal methods from previously
357 published articles. This was done to compare the difference of previous approaches.
358 We did not intend the results to be interpreted to evidence for the relationship
359 between ACWR and health problem itself.
360 Declarations
361 Acknowledgments
Copyright © ${year} Journal of Orthopaedic & Sports Physical Therapy®. All rights reserved.

367 assessors, and to all the players and coaches who participated in the study.
17
368 The authors would like to acknowledge Adam Sullivan in helping us with initial
369 EWMA calculations and Eirik Halvorsen Wik for valuable feedback on the draft
370 manuscript.
371 Funding

 "audiences":["Research & Analytics","Performance","Athletic Training"],

 "populations":["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary":"A narrative review of accelerometer-based load metrics (PlayerLoad, Body Load, Dynamic Stress Load) from upper back-mounted GNSS units in team sports. The authors report that reliability is mostly high to very high with good coefficients of variation for many outputs, while validity against motion capture and ground reaction force varies with filtering, device and activity. Links to internal load and injury are mixed, with one rugby league study finding only a moderate association between 4-week PlayerLoad accumulation and injury probability.",
 "screeningLimitations":"The review describes no search strategy or inclusion criteria, so the evidence base cannot be checked for completeness. Most validity and reliability data come from single devices, specific filters and short activity protocols, and the authors note that internal biomechanical load is rarely measured.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff may treat PlayerLoad or Dynamic Stress Load as valid measures of tissue load or injury risk, when the review finds the injury and internal-load links are weak or mixed and the metrics are not comparable across devices, manufacturers or athletes.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2024,
   "citation":"Dawson L, Beato M, Devereux G, McErlain-Naylor SA. A Review of the Validity and Reliability of Accelerometer-Based Metrics From Upper Back-Mounted GNSS Player Tracking Systems for Athlete Training Load Monitoring. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2024;38(8):e460-e475.",
   "doi":"10.1519/jsc.0000000000004835",
   "abstract":"Athlete load monitoring with upper back-mounted GNSS player tracking is common in team sports, and accelerometer-based metrics may add information that GNSS alone cannot provide. This review appraises the validity and reliability of these accelerometers and their metrics (for example PlayerLoad, Dynamic Stress Load and Body Load). Reliability depends on equipment model, signal processing and activity. Upper back placement may be suboptimal for estimating mechanical load. Validity has mostly been judged against other load and intensity measures, with correlations that vary in size and certainty. Metrics should not be compared between athletes or manufacturers, and further study is needed on links to biomechanical load pathways.",
   "tldr":"Upper back-mounted GNSS accelerometer metrics are generally reliable within the same device, but their validity depends on filtering, device and activity. Do not compare them between athletes or manufacturers.",
   "methods":"A narrative review of accelerometer-based metrics from upper back-mounted GNSS units in team sports. The authors describe the published equations for PlayerLoad, Body Load (including the New Body Load variant) and Dynamic Stress Load, then tabulate validity studies against motion capture and ground reaction force (raw and filtered data) and reliability studies (CV and ICC). The paper describes no search strategy or inclusion criteria.",
   "findings":"Reliability of GNSS-housed accelerometer data is largely high to very high, with mostly good CVs, though some studies show moderate correlations and moderate to poor CVs. Raw signals are generally less valid than filtered ones, and metrics correlate moderately to very highly with distance and heart rate but only weakly with blood lactate. In rugby league, a 4-week PlayerLoad accumulation had a moderate association with injury probability (AUC 0.585, 95% CI 0.482-0.672), while 2- and 3-week accumulations did not.",
   "limitations":"The review describes no search method or inclusion criteria, so study selection cannot be judged. The authors note that validity depends on manufacturer, processing, filtering and activity, that vertical acceleration can mask collision accelerations in rugby, and that links to internal biomechanical load are rarely studied. Upper back placement may be suboptimal for estimating whole-body mechanical load.",
   "practicalImplications":"Use the same device for repeated comparisons, and avoid comparing athletes or manufacturers directly. Set filtering and the size of a meaningful change using the reported CVs and check that the metric fits the activity, such as using PlayerLoadSlow or a 2D Body Load for rugby collisions. Do not treat these metrics as measures of tissue load or injury risk on the strength of this review.",
   "athleteDev":"Performance Application: the review supports within-device, within-athlete trend monitoring of acceleration load across training, including sprint and change-of-direction demands, because metrics track running speed and direction changes. It does not support comparing athletes or manufacturers, and it does not show that any metric guides training design.",
   "rtp":"Limited. The review reports one rugby league association between a 4-week PlayerLoad accumulation and injury probability (moderate AUC), and notes that both increased and decreased values have been linked to injury risk. It cannot be used to set return-to-play load thresholds or judge tissue readiness."
 }
}

Abstract
Dawson, L, Beato, M, Devereux, G, and McErlain-Naylor, SA. A review of the validity and reliability of accelerometer-based metrics
from upper back–mounted GNSS player tracking systems for athlete training load monitoring. J Strength Cond Res 38(8):
e460–e475, 2024—Athlete load monitoring using upper back–mounted global navigation satellite system (GNSS) player tracking is
common within many team sports. However, accelerometer-based load monitoring may provide information that cannot be
achieved with GNSS alone. This review focuses on the accelerometer-based metrics quantifying the accumulation of accelerations
as an estimation of athlete training load, appraising the validity and reliability of accelerometer use in upper back–mounted GNSS
player tracking systems, the accelerometer-based metrics, and their potential for application within athlete monitoring. Reliability of
GNSS-housed accelerometers and accelerometer-based metrics are dependent on the equipment model, signal processing
methods, and the activity being monitored. Furthermore, GNSS unit placement on the upper back may be suboptimal for
accelerometer-based estimation of mechanical load. Because there are currently no feasible gold standard comparisons for field-
based whole-body biomechanical load, the validity of accelerometer-based load metrics has largely been considered in relation to
other measures of training load and exercise intensity. In terms of convergent validity, accelerometer-based metrics (e.g., Play-
erLoad, Dynamic Stress Load, Body Load) have correlated, albeit with varying magnitudes and certainty, with measures of internal
physiological load, exercise intensity, total distance, collisions and impacts, fatigue, and injury risk and incidence. Currently,
comparisons of these metrics should not be made between athletes because of mass or technique differences or between
manufacturers because of processing variations. Notable areas for further study include the associations between accelerometer-
based metrics and other parts of biomechanical load-adaptation pathways of interest, such as internal biomechanical loads or
methods of manipulating these metrics through effective training design.
Key Words: PlayerLoad, Dynamic Stress Load, Body Load, acceleration, biomechanical load

{
 "id":"Q04",
 "sourceFile":"A systematic review and meta-analysis of wearable satellite system technology for liner sprint profiling - Technological innovations and practical applications.pdf",
 "decision":"INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason":"",
 "degradedReason":"",
 "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"Title in text 'A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Wearable Satellite System Technology for Linear Sprint Profiling: Technological Innovations and Practical Applications' matches the filename (which misspells 'linear' as 'liner') and the Crossref title; authors Cormier P et al., Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research.",
 "confidence":"high",
 "studyDesign":"Systematic Review / Meta-analysis",
 "primaryDomain":"Monitoring & Technology",
 "domains":["Monitoring & Technology","Training & Performance"],
 "audiences":["Research & Analytics","Performance","Athletic Training"],
 "sports":["Mixed / General Sport","Track & Field","Soccer","Rugby","Ice Hockey","Other Sport"],
 "populations":["Mixed / Unspecified","Male Athletes","Female Athletes"],
 "evidenceSummary":"A systematic review with meta-analysis of 16 concurrent validity and reliability studies of GNSS sensors for linear sprint profiling in athletes from recreationally trained to elite level (PubMed and SPORTDiscus, searched to July 2023). Against radar or laser criteria, pooled standardized mean differences were small for maximal sprint speed (d = 0.22, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.42), V0, relative F0 and relative Pmax, with heterogeneity moderate to high. The authors report that sampling rate and manufacturer influenced results, and that acceleration-derived metrics (t, F0) showed weaker agreement and reliability than speed metrics.",
 "screeningLimitations":"Only 16 small studies were retained, the meta-analysis used radar- or laser-criterion data only, and heterogeneity was high across devices, filters, protocols and criteria. Several manufacturers' processing steps are undisclosed, so the pooled estimates cannot be applied to a specific device without checking its own validity.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff may read the small pooled effects as proof that any GNSS device gives valid sprint-profile metrics, when the authors show that acceleration-based outputs (t, F0, Pmax) have weak agreement and reliability and depend on sampling rate, filtering and manufacturer.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2023,
   "citation":"Cormier P, Meylan C, Agar-Newman D, Geneau D, Epp-Stobbe A, Lenetsky S, et al. A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Wearable Satellite System Technology for Linear Sprint Profiling: Technological Innovations and Practical Applications. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2023.",
   "doi":"10.1519/jsc.0000000000004689",
   "abstract":"An emerging practice is the use of GNSS technology to profile team-sports athletes in training and competition. This narrative systematic review with meta-analysis evaluated satellite sensor usage for sprint modeling and its validity and reliability. Sixteen studies were retained from 1,485 identified. Effects were expressed as standardized mean differences between GNSS-derived and criterion (radar and laser) values for maximal sprint speed, acceleration constant, maximal theoretical velocity, relative force and relative power; all were small. No publication bias was found, sampling rate and sensor manufacturer moderated results, and heterogeneity was moderate to high. The authors conclude that all-out linear sprints with GNSS can be integrated into sessions when robust and consistent processing is used.",
   "tldr":"GNSS sprint modeling shows small pooled differences from radar or laser for top-speed metrics, but acceleration-based outputs are less reliable. Use devices sampling at 10 Hz or more, report processing steps, and treat acceleration metrics with caution.",
   "methods":"Following PRISMA, the authors searched PubMed and SPORTDiscus up to 1 July 2023 using GNSS, GPS, accelerometer and IMU terms with sprinting, team sports and athletes, plus reference lists. Eligible studies were concurrent validity or reliability studies of GNSS linear sprint outputs in athletes, in English and peer reviewed; the protocol was registered on the Open Science Framework. Study quality used a modified Downs and Black checklist, and a mixed-effects meta-analysis of radar or laser criterion studies pooled SMDs, with moderator analyses for sampling rate (10 Hz or more vs under 10 Hz) and manufacturer.",
   "findings":"Sixteen studies were included, most with radar or laser criteria, and funnel plots and Egger tests showed no publication bias. Pooled SMDs were small for maximal sprint speed (d = 0.22, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.42, I2 = 55%), t (d = -0.18, 95% CI -0.60 to 0.23, I2 = 87%), V0 (d = 0.14), relative F0 (d = 0.15) and relative Pmax (d = 0.21). Sampling rates under 10 Hz and some manufacturers showed moderate overestimation of speed, and CVs were under 5% for MSS, V0 and relative Pmax but over 5% for F0 and t.",
   "limitations":"The meta-analysis includes only radar and laser criteria, and many studies used small samples, filtered or raw data inconsistently, and under-reported filter settings. Several included studies used timing gates as the criterion, which the authors say may not suit acceleration-based comparisons, and only two databases were searched. The year 2023 is as printed in the PDF; the Crossref record gives 2024, so the PDF year is used.",
   "practicalImplications":"Sprint profiling with GNSS is reasonable for top-speed metrics when the device samples at 10 Hz or more and the same device and processing are used across sessions. Staff should not rely on GNSS t, F0 or Pmax as precise measures of acceleration capacity, and should record the sampling rate, filtering, onset and end-of-sprint rules, and satellite quality with every profile.",
   "athleteDev":"Performance Application: the review supports using standardized all-out linear sprints within training to build force-velocity profiles and track changes in top speed, with best use when the same device and processing are used across time. It does not show that acceleration-based profile metrics detect small training changes reliably.",
   "rtp":"Limited. The review covers healthy trained athletes and does not test sprint profiles after injury. Its suggested rehabilitation use is a general concept, so it cannot be used to set sprint-based return-to-sport criteria or judge readiness from acceleration metrics."
 }
}

Abstract
Cormier, P, Meylan, C, Agar-Newman, D, Geneau, D, Epp-Stobbe, A, Lenetsky, S, and Klimstra, M. A systematic review and meta-
analysis of wearable satellite system technology for linear sprint profiling: technological innovations and practical applications. J
Strength Cond Res XX(X): 000–000, 2023—An emerging and promising practice is the use of global navigation satellite system
(GNSS) technology to profile team-sports athletes in training and competition. Therefore, the purpose of this narrative systematic
review with meta-analysis was to evaluate the literature regarding satellite system sensor usage for sprint modeling and to
consolidate the findings to evaluate its validity and reliability. Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and
Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines, an electronic search of the databases, PubMed and SPORTDiscus (EBSCO), was conducted.
Concurrent validity and reliability studies were considered, and 16 studies were retained for the review from the initial 1,485 studies
identified. The effects on outcomes were expressed as standardized mean differences (SMDs, Cohen’s d) for each outcome
(i.e., maximal sprint speed [MSS], the acceleration constant [t], maximal theoretical velocity [V0], relative force [F0], and relative

resulted in the following estimates: small for MSS (d 5 0.22, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.42), t (d 5 20.18, 95% CI 20.60 to 0.23), V0 (d 5
0.14, 95% CI 20.08 to 0.36), relative F0 (d 5 0.15, 95% CI 20.25 to 0.55), and relative Pmax (d 5 0.21, 95% CI 20.16 to 0.58). No
publication bias was identified in meta-analyzed studies and moderator analysis revealed that several factors (sampling rate and
sensor manufacturer) influenced the results. Heterogeneity between studies was considered moderate to high. This highlighted the
differences between studies in sensor technology differences (i.e., sampling rate, sensor fusion, and satellite network acquisition),
processing techniques, criterion technology used, sprint protocols, outcome reporting, and athlete characteristics. These findings
may be useful in guiding improvements in sprint modeling using GNSS technology and enable more direct comparisons in future
research. Implementation of all-out linear sprint efforts with GNSS technology can be integrated into sport-specific sessions for
sprint modeling when robust and consistent data processing protocols are performed, which has important implications for fatigue
monitoring, program design, systematic testing, and rehabilitation in individual and team sports.
